"Right now, for example, in the area of a long-range ballistic missile that can hit a moving target, this has been one of our challenges, which, thank God, has been accomplished in the past few days, and further successes are on the way," he added.

He did not say what moving target Iranian ballistic missiles had allegedly hit, but several ships have been struck by unknown projectiles this week in and around the Strait of Hormuz, according to the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center.

Flights to and from Tehran's main international airport have fallen by 42% since the U.S. imposed sanctions that forbid other countries and entities from supporting Iranian airlines a week ago, but some popular routes remain active, according to tracking data up to Wednesday.

On average, 53 daily international flights have operated to and from Tehran's Imam Khomeini International Airport since Sept. 23, when the U.S. measures took effect - part of a wider campaign to increase economic pressure on the Iranian regime.

That is down from a daily average of 91 international flights in and out of Tehran before the sanctions were imposed, according to data from tracking platform FlightRadar24 cited by the AFP.

The U.S. threatened countries and entities that do not comply with its sanctions with expulsion from the U.S. dollar-based global financial system.

Iranian air traffic had already fallen in the wake of the U.S. and Israel launching strikes on the country at the end of February, which temporarily closed Iran's airspace. Since flights resumed, only Iranian carriers have operated services out of Iran.

Since the U.S. ban, flights have completely stopped to Georgia, Oman and Azerbaijan, which previously had regular services to Tehran. On other routes, traffic has been greatly reduced.

No flights have taken off between Iraq and Tehran since September 25 but Iraq's transport ministry said Tuesday that the U.S. had given permission for its national carrier to operate flights between the holy city of Najaf and Iran. They are set to start in October.

Flights to and from China have stayed the same at eight flights per day, on average.

President Trump has said the kingdom of Saudi Arabia "wouldn't be here right now" if it wasn't for him, while reiterating the same claim about Israel.

In an interview with TIME magazine published Thursday, the president was asked about his relationship with Saudi Arabia, after CBS News and other outlets reported that he had turned down a request from the kingdom to join Saudi forces in bombing the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.

"Good," Mr. Trump said of his ties with Saudi leaders. "I've done a lot for Saudi Arabia. I protect Saudi Arabia. If I weren't president, Saudi Arabia wouldn't be here right now. Neither would Israel. They'd be wiped off the face of the planet."

"I like the crown prince," he added, referring to Mohammed Bin Salman. "My relationship is very good. But remember, if I weren't here, there wouldn't be a Saudi Arabia. There wouldn't be an Israel. There wouldn't be various other countries, also."

Iran's Mission to the United Nations in New York said its delegation left the city on Monday evening as scheduled, rejecting reports that it had been asked by the United States to leave.

The mission said the departure had been planned in advance and that the schedule had been communicated to the U.S. Department of State on Sept. 17.

Axios reported Wednesday that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had asked the delegation on Monday to leave New York after negotiations between the two nations, carried out via mediators, stalled, citing a U.S. official and a second source with knowledge of the matter.

"Having achieved nothing, the State Department has resorted to propagating baseless and worthless news," Iran's mission said in a post on X about the reported request from Rubio.

Emirates has suspended all of its codeshare flights with FlyDubai to Tel Aviv, meaning people who booked to fly to Israel through the Emirates – which always requires a change in Dubai – will no longer be able to board the first leg of their journey.

"Passengers whose final destination is Tel Aviv will not be accepted for travel at the point of origin," said the UAE government-owned airline in a statement Thursday, adding that "customers already en route to Tel Aviv will be accommodated and provided with all possible support to complete their journeys."

FlyDubai flights from Tel Aviv have been suspended amid investigations into the alleged attempt on Wednesday by a FlyDubai co-pilot to crash a plane carrying more than 170 people, most of them Israelis, after stabbing the captain.

Passengers were able to subdue the attacker, believed to be an Omani national, and the plane made a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

Passenger Ron Levi told CBS News on Wednesday "it was the most frightening experience we've ever had in our lives."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said the co-pilot underwent "Islamist radical indoctrination," but he told CBS News on Wednesday that it was "too early to say whether there was Iranian collusion here. I think we'll find out, won't take a long time."

Israel warned Britain that Iran was planning an attack on an air base weeks before five men were arrested on Sunday near a base in England used by the U.S. forces to launch strikes on Iran, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said, as he denounced the U.K. government for pressuring his own administration over the treatment of Palestinians.

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday there were "strong indications" that Iran was involved in suspicious activity near the RAF Fairford air base, which led to the arrests on Sunday. The release on bail of the five men the following day, without any criminal charges, was criticized by President Trump.

Netanyahu, speaking to Fox News late Wednesday, said Israel had given Britain information about a plot shortly before Burnham's government, on Sept. 8, joined 11 other nations in announcing sanctions on products from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

"You want to hear how absurd things are there, and how far the anti-Israel propaganda has gone?" Netanyahu told the U.S. network's conservative host Sean Hannity. "We gave the Brits the intel that there was going to be an attack, and it's an Iranian-sponsored attack. And pretty much the next day, they slapped sanctions on us."

President Trump earlier spoke of a possible Iranian role in the incident near the British base, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that it "clearly involved" a foreign actor, without offering any evidence.

The nature of the incident remains unclear, and police have said no viable explosives or weapons were discovered. The men, who arrived in a rural village near the base in the dead of night in three vehicles, had large plastic drums, many appearing empty from aerial video, and a quantity of gasoline.

According to British media, one of the five men called the police himself about an hour before they were reported by a resident. Police said Monday that the men could have been, "either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state."

Since taking office in late July, Burnham has taken a tougher stance on Israel, saying his predecessor did not do enough.

President Trump has told TIME magazine the United States could resume its military campaign against Iran after the midterm elections if Tehran and Washington fail to reach a satisfactory agreement, and that he doesn't think "you could ever have peace" with Iran.

In an interview published Thursday, Mr. Trump said he had initially expected the war to last six to eight weeks, but that he decided to continue the campaign after what he described as the destruction of Iran's nuclear capabilities, saying he didn't want "to have [the regime] come back in some different form."

The president said the U.S. had destroyed Iran's navy, air force and radar systems, and that "they have no money."

He also told the magazine he had rejected Iran's latest peace proposal partly because they only offered to open "some aspects of" the Strait of Hormuz. "It's just not good enough, nearly," he said.

Mr. Trump said U.S. military action against Iran - which has largely halted in recent weeks - could resume and continue if necessary, arguing that "by annihilating Iran, we've created peace in the world."

"With Iran, I don't think you could ever have peace," he added.

Asked if he would order new strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections, he said it was "possible," and added: "We have a lot of weapons," renewing a threat he issued over the weekend.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi on Thursday confirmed June 30, 2027, as the new deadline for armed factions in the country - many of which are backed by Iran - to turn over their weapons to the state, following the end of the U.S.-led coalition's mission in the country. Iraq had previously set Sept. 30 this year as the deadline for the groups' disarmament, hoping for it to coincide with the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the country.

That previous deadline, according to al-Zaidi, is now a starting point.

"October 1 is considered a serious beginning to address the issue of weapons outside state control ... according to a clear roadmap and agreed timelines extending no later than June 30, 2027," he said in a statement. He had told The New York Times last week that the groups should be disbanded by June 2027.

The Iraqi government believes the withdrawal of coalition forces will deprive the armed factions, including Shiite Muslim groups considered proxies of Iranian power, of the excuse they have used to retain their arsenal.

But many fear the pullout could boost the factions instead, and draw the country deeper into the Iran war.

"The majority of Iraqis doubt the ability of the security and military apparatus to maintain security in the country, whether regarding the prevention of external aggressions and attacks or internal movements by armed groups operating outside state control of the government," journalist and regional political analyst Saman Noah told CBS News on Wednesday.

That is "especially true given that experience has proven the government's inability to subject these [Iran-backed] groups to state decision-making, control their behavior or hold their members accountable," he said.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which has long worked directly and openly with some of the Iraqi factions, welcomed the U.S. withdrawal from Iraq as a "historic victory" and vowed to "continue to stand alongside the peoples of the region who seek justice and oppose oppression."

In July, the U.S. and Saudi militaries launched airstrikes on Iranian-backed groups in Iraq after they allegedly targeted American forces in the region.

A senior Israeli official told CBS News' Dov Lieber on Thursday that United Arab Emirates President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan personally told Israeli premier Benjamin Netanyahu on Wednesday that he expected Saudi authorities to transfer the co-pilot of the FlyDubai flight who stabbed his colleague mid-air to the UAE for questioning.

According to Israeli officials, the FlyDubai jet was about two hours into its flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday when the co-pilot, who has not been identified but is believed to be of Omani nationality, stabbed the captain and tried to crash the jet with dozens of mostly Israeli passengers onboard.

Israeli officials and passengers have said the captain, an Indian national, was able to fight off his co-pilot and unlock the cockpit door. Witnesses recounted how a group of passengers and crew members then stormed the cockpit and subdued the co-pilot.

Netanyahu told CBS News on Wednesday that he assumed the co-pilot would be "moved very quickly to Dubai," adding that Israeli authorities would "join the interrogation and find out what happened there exactly."

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has welcomed the departure of U.S. forces from Iraq, calling it a "historic victory" and a result of the Iraqi people's resistance and determination to preserve their independence.

The IRGC "congratulates the proud people of Iraq, the united Islamic Resistance Front and the revolutionary fighters of the Islamic world on this historic victory," the IRGC said in a statement.

The U.S. Department of Defense announced the end of its two-decade deployment in Iraq on Wednesday, declaring "the successful conclusion" of its 12-year Operation Inherent Resolve mission against the ISIS terror group in the country.

The withdrawal was agreed to by U.S. and Iraqi authorities in 2024, and both governments voiced confidence Wednesday in the Iraqi security forces' ability to maintain security and control over extremist groups on their own going forward.

The IRGC, however, framed it as the result of Iraqi resistance and accused Washington of causing insecurity, terrorism and instability across the region during two decades of military intervention. It said the Iraq withdrawal should be followed by an end to all U.S. and Israeli military involvement in the region.

"America must leave the region and leave the management of security to the peoples themselves," the IRGC said.

The U.S. says Iran is desperate and continued to show it with what Iran's military called a "letter to the American people."

A spokesperson for Iran's powerful Revolutionary Guard Corps, Gen. Hossein Mohebbi, read from the letter at a news conference Tuesday, saying the only way for the war with Iran to end is for Washington to admit defeat and for U.S. forces to leave the region.

But a State Department spokesperson said in a statement to CBS News Wednesday night that "the IRGC's desperate effort to lie to the American people does not change the hard facts about the Iranian regime's record of maliciousness both in Iran and abroad.

"Iran, the leading state sponsor of terrorism, continues to choose terror over prosperity, and ordinary Iranians pay the price."

The spokesperson said that "despite these latest lies coming from the regime, the facts remain: U.S. operations have significantly destroyed the regime's defense industrial base, navy, and air force and shattered Iran's missiles, missile launchers, every day vessels from around the world transit through the Strait of Hormuz under the guard of American forces, bringing energy to the world despite Iran's reckless disregard for freedom of navigation and international commerce.

"This false letter, the Iranian regime's latest act of desperation, is nothing more than a smoke screen, and the world sees it for what it is."

Olivia Gazis contributed to this report.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told an Iranian delegation to depart the U.S. a day earlier than planned, a U.S. official and diplomatic source told CBS News.

The U.S. order to leave was given Monday following technical talks between U.S. and Iranian officials, the sources said.

The delegation, led by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, came to New York last week for the United Nations General Assembly and held indirect talks with the U.S. to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Araghchi had previously told CBS News he was already scheduled to depart on Tuesday.

The U.S. has not expelled all Iranian diplomats who are assigned to the U.N. and are based on U.S. soil.

Asked by reporters Wednesday how he plans to deal with Iranian officials he has repeatedly described as "crazy," President Trump offered: "Maybe you blow them up."

"We have to make that decision: We blow them up or make a deal," the president said. "But the time is coming. It's going to end very soon, one way or another."

Mr. Trump's plans for Iran remain unclear. He has said repeatedly in recent weeks that he is weighing whether to escalate the war or cut a deal with Iran.

A music festival in Saudi Arabia announced in an email to ticket holders Wednesday it was being postponed, becoming the latest entertainment event to be nixed amid the ongoing Middle East war.

"We know we said we'd see you at Soundstorm this year, so this isn't the update we wanted to share. With regret, Soundstorm '26 will be postponed," read the email from the organizers of MDLBEAST Soundstorm festival.

The announcement to cancel the December festival comes a month after an upcoming UAE concert by singer Christina Aguilera and a separate Abu Dhabi festival featuring Shakira were both canceled.

Bruno Mars, DJ Khaled and Cardi B are among the most popular international artists to have performed during past iterations of the Soundstorm festival in the Saudi capital. The lineup for this year's festival had not yet been announced.

Bahrain, a regular target of attacks by Iran in the wake of the Israeli- and U.S.-launched war, has joined the U.S.-led multinational drone task force, U.S. Central Command said Wednesday.

"We're excited to welcome Bahrain to Task Force Falcon Strike after the kingdom affirmed its commitment to join CENTCOM in building the world's first multinational attack drone unit," Central Command Cmdr. Adam Cooper said in a statement. "Bahrain is a steadfast partner in strengthening regional security and stability."

Task Force Falcon Strike was launched in August to advance one-way drone development in the Middle East. At the time of the launch, the U.S. said it and other regional partners would "employ one-way attack drones consisting of unmanned systems from above, on, and below the sea."

It is unclear whether other countries have joined the unit prior to Bahrain.

Bahrain has come under fire from Iran regularly since the war began. On the first day of the war, Iran targeted the headquarters for the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet. While no one was killed, the base suffered severe damage.

Iran also targeted Bahrain's Sheikh Isa Air Base, which houses U.S. troops, and several civilian buildings throughout March and April. The attacks have gradually declined in recent months.

Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi says the Suez Canal has lost a cumulative $20 billion in revenue since the Hamas-led attack on Israel unleashed the war in Gaza on Oct. 7, 2023, and because of maritime navigation disruptions from the Middle East conflict.

During a televised meeting on Tuesday with Cabinet members, top military leaders and local governors, el-Sissi blamed the government's tight budget and little spending on education and health on the volatile geopolitical situation that led to increases in food and energy prices.

"Does that affect us? Of course it does affect us severely," el-Sissi said.

Traffic was significantly disrupted after Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels began targeting vessels heading to Israel through the Suez Canal after the start of the war in Gaza. Since then, traffic has remained between 60% and 70% below prewar levels, according to a July report by the Oxford Economics research firm.

Alternate export routes and a U.S.-protected route through the Strait of Hormuz have helped restore oil and fuel exports from the Gulf to near prewar levels, according to figures from data firm Kpler.

Exports through the Red Sea and the Suez Canal — along with a pipeline to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman and a U.S.-protected route that guides tankers at night — have been a key workaround after the threat of Iranian attacks disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, Kpler said during a Tuesday podcast.

About 21.8 million barrels per day of crude and fuel products made from crude are being shipped weekly, on average, compared to the prewar baseline of 23.3 million barrels per day, Kpler said.

"We are getting closer to the norm, we are not at pre-conflict levels, but we are getting close to there," said Matt Smith, Kpler's director of commodity research.

Still, the workarounds are time consuming and expensive.

The British government believes Iran "played a part" in the incident over the weekend at the RAF Fairford air base in England, which has been used by U.S. warplanes carrying out strikes on Iran, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday.

Burnham's remarks to the BBC were the first confirmation by the British government of its assessment of the incident, which saw five men — all British nationals in their mid-20s — arrested near RAF Fairford early Sunday morning on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. They were all released on bail the following day, however, even though the police had the right to hold them for up to 14 days under U.K. counterterrorism laws.

Their quick release drew criticism from President Trump and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. But it also prompted questions in the U.K. as to whether the authorities had overreacted.

Top Lebanese officials, including President Nawaf Salam and Foreign Minister Youssef Raggi, met with the Senate Foreign Relations Committee on Wednesday to discuss reclaiming land from the Iran-backed Hezbollah militia.

"The discussion focused on the government's efforts to restore Lebanon's sovereignty and extend state authority across its entire territory, as well as progress on reforms and economic recovery," Raggi said in a statement.

Sens. Jim Risch, Jeanne Shaheen, Chris Coons and Tim Kaine met with the Lebanese leaders.

Hezbollah has grown in power and political influence in Lebanon since the 1990s and consistently launched operations against Israel. The group launched strikes into Israel in March in the wake of Israeli and U.S. attacks on Iran.

As part of a trilateral agreement signed between the U.S., Israel and Lebanon in late June, official Lebanese forces were supposed to progressively take over security from Israel, which invaded southern Lebanon in response to the strikes from Hezbollah. Israel, however, has resisted, saying it needs Hezbollah to completely disarm beforehand.

Iraqi armed factions backed by Tehran said Wednesday they were "not bound by any timeline or agreement" to surrender their weapons to the state, as the government seeks to disarm them under mounting U.S. pressure.

A military spokesman for Kataeb Hezbollah, Jaafar al-Husseini, said at an event to celebrate the withdrawal of U.S.-led coalition forces that the factions had been in talks on "regulating" their weapons but "have not yet received a response from the Iraqi government."

"Based on this, the Islamic Resistance declares that it is not bound by any timetable or agreement that any governmental or political party has spoken of or may speak of," al-Husseini said.

The U.S. military announced on Wednesday it had officially pulled out of Iraq after 12 years fighting the Islamic State. The U.S. and Iraqi government had agreed to a pullout by Sept. 30 and began the process over recent months.

The militias in Iraq have launched attacks on other Gulf countries in the wake of the U.S. and Israeli launching war on Iran in February. The U.S. and Saudi Arabia launched joint strikes on those militias in late July.

A British maritime agency said Wednesday that unknown projectiles struck three ships in the Strait of Hormuz the previous day. A crude oil tanker and two other vessels had each "been struck by an unknown projectile," the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center (UKMTO) said.

It had earlier described one of the vessels as an LNG tanker, before later describing it as a tanker.

The Strait of Hormuz is at the center of the war between Iran and the United States.

Around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas passed through the strategic shipping lane before the war. But since the conflict broke out, Tehran has been attempting to block the passage of commercial ships, firing on vessels it accuses of unauthorized crossings.

Washington has responded with a counterblockade of Iranian ports in an effort to prevent Tehran from exporting its oil.

An Iranian woman sentenced to death over protests earlier this year has begged the international community to save her life and those of others facing the death penalty, according to an audio message she sent from prison that was shared Wednesday by rights groups.

The plea by Mahboubeh Shahbani, 33, from a prison in the eastern Iranian city of Mashhad, came after authorities executed two more men on charges linked to the major anti-regime protests in January.

Rights groups accuse Iran of ramping up executions of high-profile prisoners in a bid to intimidate the population and ensure there is no repeat of the protests, which preceded the U.S. and Israel launching their joint war against the Islamic republic on Feb. 28.

Iran more than doubled its use of executions in 2025, Amnesty International said earlier this year.

"The sentence handed down to me shows that many others are in danger of execution," Shahbani said in a telephone call from the phone for prisoners in Mashhad's Vakilabad prison.

"I am not worried about myself. I am worried for the others whose sentences have been upheld," she said in the call, an audio recording of which was shared by Norway-based Iran Human Rights (IHR) and the U.S.-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).

It was not immediately possible to verify the authenticity of the message.

"I call on everyone - the public, the U.N., human rights organizations. Not just for me but for all the others whose sentences have been upheld and who have spent months sleeping in fear and stress at night," she said. "I call on them to do something."

According to the U.S.-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), Shahbani was convicted of carrying out actions "to strengthen Israel, the U.S., and individuals affiliated with opposition groups" in the protests.

IHR said she had merely used her motorcycle to transport injured protesters.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said lasting security in the Persian Gulf and its waterways depends primarily on cooperation among, and is the responsibility of regional countries, in a message marking World Maritime Day.

"The Strait of Hormuz, as one of the most important maritime passages, has a special position in the security and economy of the region and the world," Pezeshkian said, according to Iranian state news agency IRNA.

"Our approach to this strategic waterway is responsible and based on maintaining the security, stability and interests of the countries of the region," he said. "We believe that lasting security in the Persian Gulf and its waterways depends, more than anything else, on the cooperation, responsibility and role of the countries of the region."

Iran has repeatedly targeted U.S. regional allies around the Gulf since the war began in late February, as well as commercial vessels it accuses of attempting to navigate the Strait of Hormuz without its permission.

Iran's semi-official Fars news agency claimed Wednesday that Iranian security agencies had received intelligence suggesting Israeli plans to orchestrate a false-flag "mass-casualty incident" to blame on the Islamic Republic.

Fars, which is linked to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said intelligence obtained by an Iranian security agency pointed to a scenario it said had been proposed by the Israeli intelligence agency Mossad to the prime minister's office involving an operation against aircraft or airports in the region.

The report claimed the plan was to "create a mass-casualty incident and provide the grounds for attributing responsibility for it to Iran."

Fars reported separately on the FlyDubai incident Wednesday that saw a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv diverted for an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a violent cockpit altercation, which some reports suggested could have started as an attempted hijacking by one crew member. The Iranian news agency did not link the FlyDubai incident to the purported intelligence about a possible Israeli false-flag operation.

The U.S. military announced on Wednesday that it has completed the withdrawal of all American troops from Iraq, ending a 12-year mission to fight the Islamic State group.

The withdrawal, agreed on two years ago, comes against the backdrop of the ongoing war between the United States and Iran that has also sometimes spilled over into Iraq, with Iran-backed militias firing on U.S. troops and the U.S. striking the groups' strongholds.

The withdrawal was celebrated by Iran-backed groups but raised concerns among some other Iraqis, particularly in the Kurdish region.

"The expulsion of the occupation forces, defeated, from the land of Iraq is the beginning of full sovereignty," Abu Mujahid al-Assaf, a security official with the powerful Kataib Hezbollah militia, said in a statement.

U.S. troops pulled out of bases in most areas of Iraq last year but maintained a small presence of hundreds of troops in the semiautonomous northern Kurdish region. Bases there have regularly come under attack since the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran on Feb. 28. Iran-backed Iraqi militias also have coordinated with Yemen's Houthi rebels to attack Saudi Arabia.

Iranian authorities said on Wednesday they received the formal U.S. response to their proposal to end the Middle East war, state media reported, days after President Trump publicly rejected the plan.

"At today's cabinet meeting, the American side's proposal was presented to President Masoud Pezeshkian by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi," government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani told the official IRNA news agency.

Pakistan will use "whatever means are available" to defend Saudi Arabia against Iran-backed Houthi rebels, the country's defense minister said Tuesday, offering one of Islamabad's clearest indications yet that it could become directly involved in the widening regional conflict.

Defense Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif declined to say whether Pakistani forces had already participated in airstrikes. He said, however, that Pakistan's military capabilities would be available to Saudi Arabia under a new mutual defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkey.

"I'm not going into detail, but obviously when I say that we are bound by this arrangement to defend Saudi Arabia, that means whatever means are available at our disposal, they'll be available to Saudi Arabia also. I think that's a categoric statement," Asif told reporters during a visit to Rome when asked whether Pakistan had been involved in airstrikes against Iranian operators in Yemen.

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi received feedback from the U.S. on the proposed plan for a seven-day cease-fire, which would be aimed at building trust between the two sides, according to an official quoted by the Reuters news agency.

Iran proposed a seven-day plan for a cease-fire and the phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz last week, contingent on the U.S. meeting conditions laid out in the mid-June memorandum of understanding that fell apart after several weeks. President Trump has publicly rejected the Iranian proposal.

According to the Reuters report, the disagreement between the two sides is currently over the sequencing of the plan, and Araghchi will discuss it in Tehran on Wednesday.

President Trump is stuck when it comes to deciding between further war and negotiations, according to Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, the head of Iran's influential Supreme National Security Council.

"We stated our conditions, but Trump is incapable of decision-making," Rezaei said Tuesday during a meeting with Azerbaijan's deputy prime minister, Shahin Mustafayev. "Trump is trapped in a quagmire where he can neither negotiate nor fight."

Multiple Iranian officials have said they are waiting for a response on the proposal made during last week's U.N. General Assembly, however, Mr. Trump already dismissed the plan on Saturday.

"Our plan, which became known as the seven-point plan, was conveyed to the Americans through the Qatari intermediary," Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told reporters in New York on Monday. "Despite the things that the American president and others said, I said that we are waiting for an official response from America through the intermediary."

Rezaei singled out the strict sanctions on airlines that went into place last week, calling them an "air blockade," as a sign of "desperation."

The U.S. Treasury Department imposed sanctions Tuesday on 10 individuals and companies accused of helping Iran's military logistics agency acquire weapons and electronics.

The targets include people based in Iran, Beijing, Hong Kong and Pakistan.

The sanctions are part of a Trump administration initiative called Operation Economic Outcast, aimed at pressuring Iran by isolating its government and economy.

"Treasury will not tolerate any support to the regime and will continue to identify, expose, and isolate Iran's enablers," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.

Iran's powerful Revolutionary Guard Corps said that the only way for the war in Iran to end is for Washington to admit defeat and leave.

IRGC spokesperson Gen. Hossein Mohebbi delivered the message at a news conference Tuesday in Tehran, reading from what he called a "letter to the American people."

The message was apparently meant for the U.S. public just weeks ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections for the U.S. Senate and Congress — a vote in which President Trump's Republican Party faces fierce headwinds as it looks to maintain control of Congress.

Later, in remarks to The Associated Press, Mohebbi urged Americans to reconsider their leadership and take to the streets and protest the president's policies to denounce what he called the U.S. government's warmongering policies.

He accused the United States of using Iran's nuclear program as a ruse to "plunder Iran's wealth" and to turn the country "back into a colony."

title: New details emerge in Cornell rape case as Letitia James takes over investigation
description:
Governor Kathy Hochul/X
New York State Attorney General Letitia James will be taking over as special prosecutor in the case alleging sexual assault at Cornell University, Gov. Kathy Hochul announced Thursday, saying she “lost faith” in the district attorney’s ability to oversee it.
The announcement comes as new details have emerged this week about the alleged gang rape of then-student Jane Doe in a room at the Chi Phi fraternity house in 2024, including what she told campus police about the alleged assault.
“New information has raised serious questions about how this case was handled, and I’ve lost faith in the Tompkins County DA’s ability to fairly oversee it,” Hochul said in a statement. “The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued.
fullText:
New York State Attorney General Letitia James will be taking over as special prosecutor in the case alleging sexual assault at Cornell University, Gov. Kathy Hochul announced Thursday, saying she “lost faith” in the district attorney’s ability to oversee it.

The announcement comes as new details have emerged this week about the alleged gang rape of then-student Jane Doe in a room at the Chi Phi fraternity house in 2024, including what she told campus police about the alleged assault.

“New information has raised serious questions about how this case was handled, and I’ve lost faith in the Tompkins County DA’s ability to fairly oversee it,” Hochul said in a statement. “The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued.”

James will now have the power to investigate the incident and, if warranted, prosecute any offenses and present evidence to a grand jury. Cornell told CNN Thursday it supports the governor’s decision.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has repeatedly told CNN that his office never received more than the Snapchat messages and a six-page investigative report before deciding not to bring charges in the case.

In the report, Doe she recounted being hit and feeling emotionally coerced into sexual activity while intoxicated.

She made a more explicit accusation of rape in a November 2024 interview with campus police – the transcript of which Van Houten told CNN his office never received.

Cornell has said police followed protocol and shared “all investigatory information” with the DA. But many questions remain about the initial investigation and what the county district attorney knew about the allegations. Here’s what we know:

Snapchat messages exchanged during the alleged assault in a group chat titled “Chi Phi Actives” include a photo of then-student Jane Doe in a room at the fraternity house, according to images of the chain obtained by CNN.

The conversations taking place on the fast-erasing messaging app suggest other photos or videos might have been recovered had there been a more thorough criminal investigation, according to a source close to the case.

CNN has previously reported messages in the group chat that stated “free p*ssy” upstairs and asked, “Shop still open?”

Additional images of messages obtained by CNN include a reference to one member “laying rn,” and other members asking, “are you guys at least naked?” and stating, “Like you can walk in and whip it out rn.”

In the three weeks between when the former student was allegedly gang raped to her describing the night to campus police, Doe appeared to wrestle with shame and her stance had evolved on whether an assault took place, according to records obtained exclusively by the New York Times and corroborated by Doe’s attorney.

In an article published Thursday, the Times cited documents from the university’s formal Title IX investigation that shed new light on how Doe initially viewed the night’s events, discussed them with her roommates and communicated with some of the men before she reported her allegations to university police.

“Ms. Doe’s internal processing went from denial, to shame and ultimately acceptance that she had been raped by people that she thought were her friends,” her attorney, Thomas P. Giuffra, told CNN Thursday. “Her reactions were a textbook reaction to trauma.”

CNN has not seen the Title IX filings, which are generally confidential and restricted to the parties involved.

Cornell’s investigation yielded hundreds of pages of emails, text messages, photos and interviews with Doe, her friends and six of the seven men she accused, according to the Times. The files also included an extensive transcript of the original police interviews with Doe, the Times reported.

After the alleged gang rape at Chi Phi fraternity that began on October 19, 2024, Doe recounted the night’s events to her roommates without identifying herself as a rape victim, the Times reported, citing the files.

The following narrative comes from the Times’ review of the Title IX files it obtained:

Doe reportedly told her two roommates the day she returned home that she had consumed ketamine and had sex with multiple men. One roommate told investigators that Jane Doe did not use the word “rape” or “assault” yet.

One roommate said she could not remember Doe saying yes to anything that occurred while another roommate said it appeared Doe was “in shock,” the roommate told investigators, “not really understanding the gravity of what she was saying.”

The next day, Doe reportedly spoke with her sorority big sister, who later told investigators “what she was going through is that she had not yet processed what had happened.”

Doe had also communicated with at least two of the men she later accused of sexual assault, according to the Times.

One reportedly sent Doe a text message which said: “I just wanted to apologize for how things went down the other night.” The sender said he and another male who was allegedly involved felt terrible and too under the influence of drugs and alcohol to “shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand.”

Doe replied to the man reassuringly, the Times reported, saying “non of the sexual stuff was illegal.”

But once she came to terms with what happened, she went to a health professional a few days after the incident, Doe’s attorney told CNN.

A heavily redacted, 99-page document obtained by CNN summarizes key evidence included in a Cornell disciplinary panel’s decision.

“I felt like bait. I felt like lions around me. It was just a totally debilitating place to be in,” Doe told Cornell investigators in a hearing months after her alleged assault at the Chi Phi fraternity, according to the panel’s findings.

While CNN has been unable to view the entire document due to redactions, it describes the heavy presence of ketamine at the fraternity house on the night of the alleged assault, as well as Doe’s reported state of mind at certain points.

Doe described the effects of ketamine as “vague consciousness,” according to the panel’s decision.

“You look like an operating human being… You don’t look dead or asleep necessarily. So, lights are on, but nobody’s home. Your brain is not functioning at its proper level,” she said.

Details previously reported by CNN describe Doe telling police she consumed ketamine on the night of the assault.

The panel’s decision also cites a recorded phone call Doe had with one of the defendants in early November 2024, where they discussed ketamine and other substances they took as the initial sexual activity began on the night of the alleged assault.

Doe started recording her phone calls after the alleged assault so she could have a “reference to the limited information she was receiving,” as she sought to process what happened, according to Giuffra.

Doe also recalled being “naked” in a fraternity house bed at some point during the night of the alleged assault while two men stood by, according to the decision. “They felt more like voyeurs than anything,” she said in a November interview with investigators.

A few days after the incident, Doe went to Cornell Health to get treated for a urinary tract infection and to get tested for sexually transmitted diseases, her attorney said.

“Ms. Doe disclosed to the treating health care professional that she contracted the UTI in a ‘traumatic way,’” Giuffra said about the October 22 visit.

“Ms. Doe’s disclosure warranted further inquiry, including a rape kit, consultation of medical professionals trained to deal with rape cases and a physical exam to document her injuries,” her attorney said. “Inexplicably, all the medical professional did was to advise Ms. Doe to ‘speak with somebody.’”

CNN asked the university for comment on Giuffra’s claims against Cornell Health. “At this time, we have no new information” beyond Cornell’s previous statements about the case, a Cornell spokesperson said Thursday.

Giuffra said Cornell Health failed to act during a critical window for obtaining evidence.

“Timing is vital for rape kits because DNA evidence is lost over time,” the attorney said. “Critically, two days after the assault, a rape kit would likely have revealed DNA which would have been significant information for a criminal investigation. However this was not offered or suggested.”

Doe’s attorney said he doesn’t know whether the trove of details from the Title IX investigation was ever given to Cornell police.

“I believe that the information was not, because what is contained in the proceedings is evidence of several crimes being committed with excellent supporting evidence,” Giuffra said in a statement to CNN.

Giuffra said his office did not give the documents to the Times – but he’s grateful someone did.

“There are strict privacy policies in Title IX proceedings and access to these documents are limited to school officials, involved parties and their lawyers,” Giuffra said in his statement. “I want it to be clear that we were not responsible for leaking these documents.”

But “frankly, I am glad it was leaked,” he said. “It just shows how badly this whole tragedy was handled from all sides. Even medical providers did not do the right thing.”

In the weeks after the alleged gang rape, interviews with Doe, her roommates and her sorority big sister describe a 20-year-old sophomore realizing the severity of the night’s events and understanding them as an alleged assault, according to the Times.

The documents reportedly detail how rumors about the alleged gang rape led her to fear reputational damage and left her humiliated.

It was an evolution of thought complicated by Doe’s history as a sexual assault survivor, the Times reports, citing the documents. In the six-page summary signed by Doe to police, she described having a prior “traumatic experience” regarding sexual intercourse.

After the alleged rape, Doe saw comments on an online forum about Greek life about Chi Phi brothers drugging and gang raping a sophomore, which she later told investigators: “That’s the first time I had ever heard the narrative change that I wasn’t a whore and that I was assaulted,” the Times reported.

On November 3, Doe texted one of the men, explicitly saying that what happened on that October night was not consensual. According to the Times, she wrote: “let’s be clear that 90% of what happened that night was not consensual. i was given more key than i can remember,” using a shorthand for ketamine, “and i know that i told u i felt uncomfortable and i didn’t know anyone in the room.”

Before going to campus police, Doe reportedly collected evidence, including photos of the bruises on her body allegedly caused by one of the men hitting her. She also had not washed the dress to save as potential evidence, the Times reports.

On November 7, Doe went to an emergency room in Ithaca, where Cornell is located, and requested a rape kit, the Times reported, citing the documents.

In a 2024 statement to Cornell police, obtained by CNN from a source familiar with the investigation, Doe recounted arriving at the Chi Phi fraternity house and dancing with one person who asked if she would be interested in participating in a threesome. Doe told police she was “pretty ok” with aspects of an initial encounter, but that later in the night she did not consent to other sexual activities, according to the six-page statement.

“I felt like I was unable to make any decisions because of how intoxicated I was,” she said in the statement. Doe said she felt like her overall intoxication level at one point was about an “8 out of 10” — which she said was the most intoxicated she had been in her life.

She described being “pretty incapacitated,” feeling uncomfortable, swatting one man’s hand away several times and being “horrified” as more men entered the room they were in. She said she “finally gave in” to one later encounter after she was asked “to have sex so many times,” according to the statement.

“To me that felt like coercion,” she said in the statement. “Also, I felt like due to my intoxication, they should have known how intoxicated I was based on how I was slurring my words.”

Doe made a more explicit accusation of rape in a separate document, according to CNN affiliate WCBS. The station obtained a transcript of a November 2024 interview with campus police from a source.

“I can say with 100% confidence I was raped,” Doe said in the transcript, according to WCBS.

CNN has not seen the transcript and has asked Cornell for a copy but has not heard back. The transcript is a separate document from the six-page statement that was submitted by the university.

Beyond alleged emotional pressure, Doe told police in the statement she was physically hit and remembered feeling hurt. “One hit in particular sent a sharp pain through me,” she said. The student also described noticing bruising on her body the following day.

Doe also said she “had become extremely uncomfortable with how this night was turning out” and thought, “if I passed out and the men had sex with me, then they could be charged with Rape,” the statement reads.

Doe told police she remembered consuming a “heavy amount” of ketamine, smoking marijuana and having “various things” poured on her body. She said she initially agreed to having drugs consumed off her body while feeling “extremely tired” but “couldn’t tell what they were pouring on me.”

Doe reported the alleged incident to Cornell police on November 8, 2024, weeks after the alleged assault, according to a civil complaint filed last month. In the days following the alleged incident, she was “traumatized, numb and unable to function or accept the horror of what had happened,” her attorney told CNN.

Cornell’s internal investigation revealed Doe planned to return to the fraternity house the following week for a Halloween party, according to two sources familiar with the school’s Title IX investigation.

But a fraternity official spoke with Doe before the party and advised her not to go, one of the sources told CNN. The source said fraternity members, Doe’s friends and Doe herself mentioned this in their testimonies during Cornell’s investigation.

“It was all part of her processing what had happened. She was still in the denial stage,” her attorney said. “She could not accept what happened to her.”

In the following days, Doe reported the October incident to Cornell police, according to her lawsuit.

Van Houten told CNN his office was not given the interview transcript before deciding no charges should be filed in the investigation.

The DA told CNN on Wednesday morning that the university had still not provided his office with the transcript. CNN had also reached out to Van Houten about whether it received the Title IX filings.

The DA said it was Doe’s six-page statement that determined no charges should be filed, adding, “Multiple prosecutors and criminal investigators reviewed Jane Doe’s statement and correctly determined the alleged facts as set forth in the statement do not constitute a crime.”

Van Houten said he learned of the more explicit allegation made in the interview when he was contacted by WCBS on Tuesday evening and said his office will be investigating the reported statements “fully.”

When reached by CNN about the DA’s comments, a Cornell University spokesperson did not specifically address the transcript but said it “shared all investigatory information” with the DA’s office.

The university likely did not break any laws if it did neglect to share all relevant documents with the DA, said former prosecutor Gary Galperin. But he said not sharing all documents would violate “all principles of what’s logical and decent.”

The DA’s comments Wednesday raised new questions about what law enforcement knew in the weeks after the alleged assault and why no criminal charges were filed.

“It is a case that, clearly, just on the face of her statement, is so complex and so nuanced,” former Westchester County District Attorney Mimi Rocah said

“If you’re an investigator trying to get at the truth, as this DA office should have been, they should have sought more information,” she added.

Van Houten canceled his scheduled appearance on CNN Wednesday evening, saying, “At this time I need to shift my focus to the investigation and to pursuing the additional evidence that has recently come to light.”

He said his office will keep the public informed of developments in the investigation and any action of the Tompkins County Grand Jury.

After Doe’s allegations, “Cornell established the Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault, comprising faculty, staff, and students, in early 2025,” the university said.

“Our goal is not simply to respond appropriately when sexual misconduct is reported, but to build a community in which sexual violence is prevented, people feel safe coming forward, those who do are supported, and individuals found responsible are held accountable.”

But some Cornell students who were on campus in 2024 said the university’s response hasn’t been enough.

“The main problem I see in the university’s response … is the lack of ownership,” said Hayden Watkins, executive vice president of the Cornell Student Assembly.

He also said the school’s task force on campus sexual assault is not representative.

“There’s been very little student voice throughout this entire process,” Watkins said. “That task force included roughly 20 individuals, but only two people were undergraduate students.”

The unfolding details of Jane Doe’s case have sparked renewed attention to the ongoing topic of sexual assault awareness and prevention on college campuses.

Doe’s attorney has said Cornell expelled two of the seven accused students while the others received lesser punishments, including suspensions, workshops or written assignments.

Cornell has countered that claim, saying “none of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement.”

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said Cornell has agreed to an outside investigation to “determine whether Cornell met every obligation to protect its students and pursue justice,” she told CNN. The university confirmed that it agreed to the investigation and declined to provide further details.

The Chi Phi national fraternity said Wednesday that it condemns sexual assault and drug and alcohol abuse, and three days after Doe filed a police report, the fraternity chapter “voted unanimously to remove the accused members from its rolls” and “recommended that our national fraternity permanently expel them,” which it said the fraternity’s Grand Council did in a subsequent meeting.

“These actions went beyond anything the law or Cornell University required of us,” the fraternity added in the statement.

The school also said it had closed that chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity in 2024, and that the chapter remains barred from campus.

It is unclear if any of the accused men are still Cornell students.

Help is available: For help in the US, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673 or chat 24/7 on online.rainn.org.

CNN’s Holly Yan, Chris Boyette, Rebekah Riess, Cindy Von Quednow, Avni Trivedi, Pamela Brown, Jake Tapper and Jeff Winter contributed to this report.

title: Euro 2016 memories aplenty - but O'Neill focused on future
description: Ukraine against Northern Ireland is a fixture which brings up plenty of memories, but Michael O'Neill is firmly focused on the future.
fullText:
Whenever Northern Ireland face Ukraine, it is inevitable that the memories start coming back.

The hailstones that halted the game, the Gareth McAuley header, Niall McGinn wheeling away in pure elation and the endless renditions of 'Will Grigg's on fire'.

Whether you were at the game or watching at home, it's hard to believe 10 years have passed since that famous day in France at Euro 2016.

But for Michael O'Neill, who was in the dugout that day in Lyon, it's not time for reflection.

He understands why fans and media want to talk about it. It is, after all, one of the most famous days in Northern Ireland's history, but his focus is firmly on what is to come.

"We don't keep reflecting back on that game and telling the players this is what we aspire to be," he told BBC Sport NI in Trnava.

"This team hopefully can write its own history and we have to allow them to do that."

Inside Northern Ireland's football conveyor belt

Can you name NI team against Ukraine at Euro 2016?

Of the squad who are in Slovakia, which is hosting the game due to the ongoing conflict between Ukraine and Russia, only two players from the Euros squad remain.

Josh Magennis and Paddy McNair - himself only 31 - are the elder statesmen of a young squad, while former Northern Ireland captain Steven Davis is now a key member of O'Neill's coaching team.

To put into context how long ago that famous day was, current squad members Ceadach O'Neill and Braiden Graham were only eight-years-old.

Even players with 25-plus caps like Trai Hume, Shea Charles, Isaac Price and Brodie Spencer were still a few years away from taking their GCSEs at that point.

The average age of the starting team in Georgia was just 23, while that dropped to just 22.5 against Hungary.

"We may use certain examples of players from those games at Euro 2016 - the likes of Steven Davis, Jonny Evans, Gareth McAuley or Stuart Dallas - as good examples for players to aspire to be.

"But for me, this team is about the future and what lies ahead."

Watch on BBC iPlayer and listen on BBC Sounds; Clips, updates and reaction on BBC Sport app and website

The ultimate aim for O'Neill is to lead his young squad to a first major tournament since 2016 when the next Euros roll around in 2028.

Their return to the second tier in the Nations League has been successful so far, with Charles scoring a 99th-minute winner in Georgia before the team showed their character with a goalless draw at home to Hungary.

The players definitely looked tired in the closing stages of the draw, which can be put down to the 5,000-mile return trip to Tbilisi, but they held their own against Dominik Szoboszlai's side.

Before that, Northern Ireland had kept Paris Saint-Germain winger Khvicha Kvaratskhelia quiet in the opener.

While Ukraine do not have the individual star power of the other teams in League B2, O'Neill knows they are still a dangerous side.

He described them as favourites on Friday night, and pointed to the fact that manager Andrea Maldera had made 10 changes between their opening 1-0 win in Hungary and the goalless draw with Georgia in their second game.

"Ukraine's strength is in their collective as a team, rather than what we faced against Georgia with Kvaratskhelia and Hungary with Szoboszlai, who are top European players.

"I think that Ukraine have many players that have potential to be on that level and go to the big, big clubs in Europe.

"We haven't highlighted any one individual, but we've looked very closely at how they play, with the ball and without the ball, and I believe their strength is in the collective of the team."

title: Wales wing Adams targets third World Cup
description: Wales wing Josh Adams is nearing full fitness in time for the autumn internationals and looking forward to a World Cup trip to Australia next year.
fullText:
Wales wing Josh Adams says he would love to play in a third World Cup as he targets a first trip to Australia next year.

It is exactly a year until Wales play their opening game against Zimbabwe in Adelaide on 2 October, before further pool games against Tonga and England.

"I'm desperate to go, but there is loads of rugby to be played and months ahead of us," said Adams, looking ahead to the tournament.

"It is important that you navigate your way through correctly and get to that start line in a good spot to be selected."

Adams, 31, was the World Cup's top try scorer in the 2019 tournament in Japan with seven as Wales reached the semi-finals.

The Cardiff back, who was also part of the squad that lost a quarter-final to Argentina four years later, insists he is just as excited for a hat-trick of global tournaments.

"I've never been to Australia, so that, as well as playing in a World Cup, is something I'm determined to do," said Adams.

Wales counting down the year until World Cup

The Warm Up: One Year To The Rugby World Cup!

Wales begin the World Cup countdown by playing four matches in the second half of the Nations Championship in November.

Japan, New Zealand and Australia will travel to play in Cardiff before a final play-off match at the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham.

Adams was ruled out of Wales' 43-0 defeat by South Africa in Durban in July due to a calf injury.

The British and Irish Lions wing has missed Cardiff's start to the season but says he will be fit for international duty next month, with a club return expected in October.

"I am training, but it's important that you navigate your way through correctly and there's no rush," said Adams.

"I had the calf injury in the summer, but I've been good for a while.

"It's making sure that when I'm playing, I'm 100% fit and healthy, and I've had good preparation time."

title: Groves' journey from heart surgery to Scarlets
description: New Scarlets lock Alex Groves describes his remarkable return to rugby following heart surgery.
fullText:
New Scarlets lock Alex Groves will make his home debut on Saturday when he lines up against the Dragons in the United Rugby Championship (URC).

The fact the 25-year-old is playing at all is remarkable considering he underwent major eight-hour heart surgery in February 2024.

There was not just a question whether he would play again. There was even concern about his survival.

"It was very scary," said Groves.

"I was confident as a young boy that I was fit and healthy and never thought anything was wrong with me. It was such a shock when I found out.

"It went very quickly from 'do I need surgery?' to 'am I still going to be playing rugby?' - to 'am I still going be alive in two years' time?'."

Carter and Costelow back for Welsh derby

Scarlets prop Domachowski ruled out for two months

Groves was born and brought up in Johannesburg but, aged 19, moved to join Bristol and would help England Under-20s win a Grand Slam.

As part of Bristol's pre-season preparations in 2021, Groves and his team-mates underwent cardio screenings unavailable to the public without symptoms. After the tests he was informed he had a leaky valve in his heart.

The 6ft 9in (2.06m) lock was told it was nothing abnormal, that one in four people have the issue, and that it would just need to be monitored.

In April 2022 Groves joined Sale Sharks, and during another similar heart screening he was told his situation had deteriorated.

The view of medical experts was that he would need surgery within the next five years to stop his heart from growing to a size where it would not be able to support itself.

On 5 January 2024, Groves' 23rd birthday, he was then told about the discovery of an aneurysm - an abnormal bulge in the wall of a blood vessel - that needed urgent attention.

"I remember they found the problem in August 2023 and from there it was on and off for a couple of months," said Groves.

"I had a test in December and then on my birthday the following year, I went in and saw my surgeon with my parents in Liverpool.

"Thank God my parents were in that meeting with me because I completely shut off and everything my surgeon told me from that point on I did not take in.

“It literally scared the life out of me and I didn't actually retain any information.

"I was on the car ride home back to Manchester and my parents were having to relay all the information.”

He recalled how an initial diagnosis had also been missed because of his unusual height.

"My surgeon said I could not play because they'd found an aneurysm that they'd missed," said Groves.

"That was purely down to the fact MRI machines aren't really built for six foot nine broad-shouldered people.

"I remember getting into that machine and sort of squishing up and by doing that, the extra body mass over my heart meant they missed it.

"But fortunately they found it because one wrong hit to the chest and I would've bled out in a matter of seconds because it was on my aortic artery."

Groves had been planning to play in a Champions Cup match for Sale against Stormers in South Africa in January but had to withdraw.

A month later he was having major surgery. He was on the operating table for eight hours.

"It was terrifying but I think it is more scary for the people closest to you," said Groves.

"I just fell asleep and woke up. But I had my girlfriend at the time and my mum sitting in the waiting room.

“I can't imagine how hard that is."

Groves said he had been put at ease by the medics before the operation.

"I remember speaking to my anaesthetist who was a big rugby fan," recalled Groves.

"He told me the procedure they were doing was as easy as it is for me as a lock to jump in the line-out.

"It's amazing they're able to do something like that at that level of ease. I thought then I'm going to be fine.

"It's amazing how advanced things have become now.

“If I was a player in my position 10 years ago they probably wouldn't have found the problem.

"Or I would have had to retire or even sadly have passed away.”

Groves spent the next nine months recovering and praised Sale for their part in helping him return to fitness.

The South African-born forward has previously spoken about his lack of motivation during that period,, external and how with different heart rhythms he was sweating and out of breath just climbing up stairs.

"It was a tough rehabilitation process," said Groves.

"Sale Sharks weren't obviously familiar with the process of a patient that has to go through open heart surgery.

"So it was a tough thing for everyone.“

Groves was given the all-clear to play again in November 2024 and was loaned out to Championship side Caldy RFC.

He returned to the field in late December in a Championship match against Ealing Trailfinders, 10 months after his surgery.

“Thankfully it was a success,” said Groves.

“I've never had a problem since. It's good as new to be honest.”

Groves left Sale in 2025 and returned to South Africa where he joined the Stormers.

He had a brief period loaned to Scarlets when they went to South Africa, Groves helping the Welsh region solve a lock-injury crisis, starting against Lions and coming off the bench against Sharks.

He joined the Llanelli club permanently for the 2026-27 season and has been embraced by some Scarlets fans his family met in Johannesburg during the Lions game - those supporters are sponsoring Groves during his stay in Wales.

They also helped him with some early accommodation when Groves spent six weeks in a flat above a pub in Llanelli, with the owners helping him settle in.

Groves, who has since moved, made his competitive debut as a replacement in the 21-15 defeat against Cardiff last weekend.

And he is enjoying his time back on the field in a new environment.

"It put things into perspective," said Groves.

"It made me realise how fortunate I am to do what I love and have the family and support I have around me.

"It sort of matured me in a way at a young age. I'm just grateful to be here still doing what I love."

title: Chris Mason: Why Andy Burnham's about-turn on Manchester City matters
description: The prime minister's comments on Man City were revealing on several levels - and leapt on by many in football, the BBC's political editor writes.
fullText:
The rows circulating around Manchester City are huge, and they are only going to get bigger.

The Premier League has concluded that City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

This, clearly, matters for the club, but that is just the start of it.

It matters for Manchester, it matters for the Premier League and so, crucially, it matters for the UK's image around the world – because England's top flight is a colossal global brand. In other words, this matters whether you like football or not.

Added to all of this, Andy Burnham pitches himself as Mr Manchester and is a big football fan.

The man who was the mayor of Greater Manchester a matter of months ago is now the prime minister, and so finds himself caught up in it all at a local level, a national level and a diplomatic level.

Diplomatic, because rows will rage over the extent to which City's ownership is separate from the Abu Dhabi state. And the state is a big UK ally.

All of this is why I thought it was in the public interest to put a series of questions to Burnham about it when I spoke to him on Wednesday as the Labour Party conference concluded in Liverpool.

His comments, in his interview with me, followed by no fewer than two attempts to backtrack 24 hours later, amount to perhaps his biggest self inflicted tangle since he arrived in Downing Street in July.

He will have expected to be asked about Manchester City, but he didn't expect sustained scrutiny about it.

One particular exchange prompted a lot of interest. I asked if he was worried that Manchester City's owners from the United Arab Emirates might sell up.

It is worth quoting his answer in full.

"Well, I would be really concerned to lose them. They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester. Obviously, the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.

"I can't intervene 

His answer is revealing on several levels, and was leapt on by many in football and then by the Conservatives, who labelled them "completely out of touch" and "extraordinary".

Firstly, his fear – being "really concerned" – that the vast money from Abu Dhabi, that has transformed not just the club but parts of the city, could go.

Secondly, that "I can't intervene more" in the process that is ongoing. What does "more" mean?

To be fair, as you can see in the full quote above and he said repeatedly elsewhere in the interview, he was trying to be circumspect about it all.

"I am not getting directly involved in the process," he told me, later adding "I have to keep my distance from it."

But, the cumulative impression many were left with was that he was sympathetic to Manchester City's situation, not least because he repeatedly compared it to a vastly smaller row involving his own club Everton's finances a few years ago.

"I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time, and you know, with hindsight, I think more people would say that wasn't fair the way that was handled. So it would be wrong of me to leap to one side given the experience that I'd had before becoming prime minister."

Everton were docked Premier League points over it.

Despite the gravity and breadth of what Manchester City now confront, Andy Burnham offered no explicit criticism of them.

The back pages and the sports channels as well as news sites and social media were quickly ablaze with the remarks.

And by teatime on Thursday, No10 were back-pedalling.

A written statement was sent out, which again is worth quoting in full:

"As the prime minister made clear, the initial judgement is serious and there can't be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules. He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected.

"If wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences."

Some 59 words that could be replaced by a picture of a reversing light – the tone and language completely different from Burnham's to me on camera.

But even that statement didn't last long. Immediately, the first word of the second paragraph of it was jumped on. "If."

Remember, the Premier League says Manchester City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of almost a billion pounds. The club deny wrongdoing and are considering an appeal, but the Premier League's conclusion is clear.

But Downing Street said "if." Fast forward a little over an hour, and the statement was re-issued. "If" became "wherever."

In real time, No10's jitters and discomfort about this was there for all to see.

The prime minister seen as Mr Manchester, who loves his football and revels in a man of the people image, caught up in one of the biggest domestic stories of the year and one that is only just beginning.

It won't be the last time he faces questions about Manchester City.

title: Browns survive late comeback to defeat Steelers
description: Andre Szmyt kicks a match-winning 56-yard field goal with 10 seconds remaining as the Cleveland Browns survive a Pittsburgh Steelers comeback.
fullText:
Andre Szmyt kicked a match-winning 56-yard field goal with 10 seconds remaining as the Cleveland Browns survived a Pittsburgh Steelers comeback in a thrilling encounter at Huntington Bank Field.

Szmyt's career-best effort, followed by a late interception by safety Grant Delpit, ensured a 27-24 victory for the Browns, who have now won three consecutive games.

The hosts led 21-10 lead at the end of the third quarter, but divisional rivals Pittsburgh fought back with Aaron Rodgers finding tight end Pat Freiermuth in the endzone before adding a two-point conversion to level the scores with one minute and 42 seconds remaining.

Cleveland quarterback Deshaun Watson, who was booed by some Browns fans in pre-season, responded by moving his team 36 yards over seven plays to set up Szmyt's winning kick.

The Steelers led 7-0 at the end of the first quarter following a Roman Wilson touchdown, but the Browns enjoyed a dominant second period to lead by 11 at half-time.

Jaleel McLaughlin and Quinshon Judkins rushed into the endzone and Harold Fannin Jr took a scoring catch, while Chris Boswell kicked a field goal for the Steelers.

A scoreless third quarter followed, before a Darnell Washington touchdown for the Steelers closed the gap.

A 44-yard field goal from Szmyt gave the Browns some breathing room, before Rodgers, who was sacked five times and intercepted twice, threw to Freiermuth to start an exhilarating conclusion.

The Browns now lead the AFC North division for the first time since November 2014, while the Steelers sit bottom with a record of two wins and two defeats.
