title: 'You could be legends' - inside unfancied Wakefield's rapid ascent
description: Wakefield Trinity's stars of yesteryear are remembered in sepia; the class of 2026 have the chance to add some colour with the chance of Grand Final glory.
fullText:
There is a moment in the 1939 film 'The Wizard of Oz' where Dorothy swaps her monochrome world for glorious, eye-opening technicolour the minute she touches down in the Land of Oz.

The same could be said for the moment, should it happen, that Wakefield Trinity get their hands on the Super League trophy this Saturday after the Grand Final against Warrington Wolves.

Metaphorically of course, but the achievements of that great club are still currently only to be seen in those black and white hues and are ripe for a dash of colour.

Derek 'Rocky' Turner, Neil Fox MBE, Don Fox, Harold Poynton, Ken Rollin... all legends of the 1960s and an era when all the silverware found its way to WF1.

Belle Vue, or the DIY Kitchens Stadium as it is now known, has had its special nights since, such as the win to relegate rivals Castleford and secure safety at their expense in 2006.

Amid all the adrenaline and excitement, that was survival. Not success.

Yet, this season poses a different storyline. Wakefield can achieve. Wakefield can be winners. Title winners, for the first time since 1968.

It is a notion that boss Daryl Powell has tapped into, as winger Tom Johnstone explains.

"Daryl put a Powerpoint presentation on the screen, and said 'You could be legends of this club', and that was it," Johnstone told BBC Radio 5 live.

"He didn't really go any further into it, he just put a seed in the back of your mind and just gave you that little nugget.

"I've been at this club for so long now and if we can be the first ones to bring success back to this club we will go down in history forever, not just at Wakefield but everywhere.

"To be the sixth name on the trophy is just massive motivation."

Warrington Wolves v Wakefield Trinity

Saturday, 3 October, kick-off 18:00 BST

Listen to commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Radio Merseyside, BBC Radio Leeds and BBC Sounds; watch highlights Saturday, 3 October from 23:00 BST on iPlayer and BBC Two on Sunday at 13:45 BST

Going back to the movie theme, Wakefield's resurrection over the past three seasons is almost too fanciful for Hollywood's scriptwriters, given the rapid ascent.

Owner Matt Ellis is without doubt the lead character, having come in as a fan but also an incredibly wealthy and successful kitchen magnate.

It has been more than just investment thrown at it; for example Ellis has been hands-on with the stadium renovation in terms of standards and finish on the back of the work of former custodians Michael Carter and John Minards who set the ball rolling.

He also has brought drive and vision, and it was he who was determined to bring Powell to the club as head coach almost immediately after taking control.

"Everything has changed from the top to the bottom," Johnstone added. "Rather than going into individual key details, the facilities have changed, the manner of the club, just the belief and the ambition of the club is probably the best one.

"We used to say a lot of things and say we wanted to compete but we had no chance of doing it at the time. Whereas now, it's an elite club. It's run so well.

"Anything you need, you've got it. Matt will provide absolutely anything. He just wants to see success. And the players we've signed and the team we've built, it just shows. It's just night and day."

Ellis and Powell has been a near-perfect partnership; with promotion back to Super League, Wembley success in the 1895 Cup, and back-to-back play-off appearances in Super League all culminating in this Old Trafford opportunity.

Powell had enjoyed success at Featherstone and Castleford before a stint at Warrington ended prematurely, and joining Wakefield has had a revitalising impact on both club and coach.

"I've been super-fortunate to get to a club that I've felt at home in straight away," Powell told BBC Sport. "Then when you feel that you can really get after your work and get the right kind of people in.

"Our coaching staff are second to none, they're unbelievable people and then get the right kind of players in, people first, players second but very good players because if you get the right people you know they're going to work hard to be the very best they can be.

"I feel like we've got all that mix right and the ownership is great which sets us up - we're just in a zone where we're all proud of each other and I know that's that's pretty special."

'Pipe dream' to reality? Wakefield one win from title

Wakefield shock Wigan to reach first Grand Final

Super League: Superb Wakefield stun Wigan to reach first Grand final - as it happened

Powell has turned to familiar faces to fill those key roles; Michael Shenton - once his captain at Castleford, is now his trusted assistant while Ste Mills - another accolyte of yore is the brains behind the recruitment.

Aside from that, former Trinity player and modern day favourite Danny Kirmond is also on the staff while the experienced Stu Dickens also adds to the brains trust.

On the pitch, Powell has reunited with Jake Trueman, whose form in his time at Castleford put him in the international picture, and Mike McMeeken, who was part of the 2017 team at the Tigers who lost to Leeds in the Grand Final.

Front-rower McMeeken's authority and presence were a huge pick up for Trinity when he signed from Catalans as a statement signing on their top flight return, part of a powerful pack which highlights the best of Mills' talentspotting.

Bringing that power are Ky Rodwell from NRL side Parramatta, and ex-Cronulla reserve grader Caleb Hamlin-Uele - both signed while Trinity were still in the Championship.

Since getting up, Caius Faatili was brought in from Queensland Cup side Sunshine Coast Falcons in 2025 and was an immediate success with his raw-boned and aggressive style; lean, muscular Isaiah Vagana is rangy and athletic in the back-row, while Samoa international Jazz Tevaga has brought NRL experience and abrasive swagger to the squad.

"Daryl's really shown how good of a coach he is just how he's brought players in that probably may not have been picked up because of not being as well known," McMeeken told BBC Sport.

"For example Caius, not many clubs would have known about him but he's seen the potential in him and the good thing is, I think he's only about 23 or 24 so it's quite scary to see how far people like him can actually go."

Will 2026 finally be Warrington Wolves' year?

Quiz: Name every Super League Grand Finalist

Without a major football club in the city, Wakefield Trinity are the prime attraction for support, and all the attention and focus has been shone on them this week.

More than 30,000 tickets have been sold for Old Trafford at Trinity's end, nudging the expected attendance past 70,000 for a showpiece that guarantees a new name on the trophy for the second year running.

Finishing fourth earned them a home eliminator where Leigh were beaten impressively, but it was the dismantling of treble-chasing Wigan in the semi-final which really caught the eye and gave growing hope that Trinity could create a seismic Super League shock.

The Wakefield club that Johnstone started out at is almost a different beast more than a decade on, for the better, but the fanbase has remained the same - committed, loyal and vocal.

"It'd mean everything to us but I think it would mean more to them," Johnstone continued.

"They've always been proud of the club but there's not been too much to be proud of in the past 20 years so it'd be amazing for them, it'd be special.

"I got stopped on the way to school with my kids the other day by someone saying 'Come on Wakefield!' and it's just good to see the club and the city going that way.

"It can only be good for rugby league and Super League for us to be growing and performing and it's finally pay back for all the loyal fans that have been here throughout the years."

It is a long time between drinks, 1968. For Wakefield, the hope is it is champagne rather than shandy they are enjoying come the final hooter on Saturday.

Yet regardless of the result, there will be immense pride. Wakefield are back, and the key for everyone at the club now is to ensure they stay there.

Saturday could be the catalyst for that. Wakefield - Wizards of Old Trafford has a ring to it, or Wizards of OT you might say.

Kim leads Asian Games seeking military exemption
description: Tom Kim tops the men's leaderboard after the third round at the Asian Games as he seeks a gold medal that will significantly reduce the time he is required to spend in South Korea's military.
fullText:
Tom Kim topped the men's leaderboard after the third round at the Asian Games as he seeks a gold medal that will significantly reduce the time he is required to spend in South Korea's military.

Having started two shots off the lead, Kim hit a brilliant five-under 65 that included five birdies and an eagle, taking him a stroke clear at 12 under par with one round to play.

Able-bodied South Korean males are usually required to undertake between 18 and 21 months of military service before the age of 28.

However the government rewards Asian Games gold medals and Olympic medals of any colour with a service exemption bar basic training, which lasts less than a month.

Athletes who have previously secured the exemption include former Tottenham footballer Son Heung-min, who served for only three weeks in 2020 having won the Asian Games two years earlier.

Kim hurried from the Presidents Cup in the United States to tee off at the Kasugai Country Club in Japan, having to manage on just six hours of sleep and a 14-hour time difference.

The 24-year-old previously came close to securing an exemption at the Paris Olympics in 2024, finishing day one tied for third before ultimately finishing eighth.

Having looked visibly emotional after that result, Kim is now chasing another chance to stop military service stalling his promising career, which has already featured an Asian Tour order of merit crown and four PGA Tour titles.

The world number 32's lead would have been larger had he not missed birdie putts on the 14th and 18th holes, but he stands clear of Taiwan's Wang Wei-hsuan, who had led overnight, and Japan's Kazuki Higa going into day four.

The men's team event title offers another route for military exemption, with South Korea also topping the men's leaderboard by one stroke.

Gold in that event will exempt Tom Kim and SH Kim, 28, regardless of the individual result, but it would come too late for the third team member, Mun Do-yeob, who has already served.

"I think about it. It's so tough," SH Kim said of the possibility of military service.

"I am 100% nervous, for sure. It's a lot of pressure. I could stay on the PGA Tour (with a gold). That's my goal."

title: Trump Is Trusting Tech Companies to Self-Police AI. What Could Go Wrong?
description: Sasha...
fullText:
Trump’s refusal to heed the warnings from within the tech industry might end up being his most asinine legacy.

Last week, Trump appeared in a bizarre 29-second campaign ad, touting a “final battle” against Marxists, warmongers, fascists, deep staters, and globalists. The voiceover, which Trump recorded during the 2024 election campaign, was accompanied by futuristic martial music, along with black and white footage of a clearly enfeebled Trump attempting to stride forcefully down the corridors of power in the White House. As the ad ended, a decal popped up: “Paid for by the US Government.” In other words, this foul half-minute of propaganda was paid for by American taxpayers.

A month out from a midterm election that in many ways will be a referendum on his presidency and on the congressional GOP’s prostituting of themselves to his sordid requirements, Trump is attempting to scare the voting public into one last MAGA hurrah. It is, of course, a Hail Mary, but he doesn’t really have a choice. These days, number 47 is catastrophically unpopular with the electorate. On almost every key measure, Americans are rejecting him. They dislike his sadistic anti-immigrant policy, view his tariffs and other economic policies as a calamity, are infuriated by high inflation, alienated by the war in Iran, distrustful of his alliance with Big Tech, angered by his cozying up to dictators and his flaying of allies, pissed at the government dysfunction wrought by DOGE, disapproving of his environmental policies, and suspicious of his efforts to purge voter rolls.

So, the sunsetting octogenarian is doing what he always does. He is seeking to stoke even more fear and even more division, in the hope that voters once again see him as a potent strongman-leader able to shake the country back into shape. Hence the unhinged black-and-white ad of Trump striding manfully, or what he hopes appears as such, along the halls of the White House while warning of a treasonous effort to hand America over to a motley crew of communists and miscellaneous other pinkos.

The ad is wrong on so, so many levels. First and foremost, there’s the obvious impropriety of using taxpayer dollars for a blatantly partisan “public announcement” like this. Trump is practically daring Congress to try to rein him in, daring the courts to enforce a slew of existing laws against using taxpayer dollars for partisan ends.

But beyond the shamelessness, there’s the actual content of the ad itself, which, in its end-time tone, is a bizarro combination: Joe McCarthy meets The X-Files meets Musk’s fascist Grok AI assistant.

Trump’s presidency is increasingly just weird. Having lost much of his base and alienated most of the rest of the world with obnoxious words and irrational, cruel acts, he has retreated into a largely AI-generated fantasy world, often activated in the middle of the night, when, presumably unable to sleep, he prowls the residential rooms of the White House and stews in rage until he can’t help himself but dive back into social media. With an assist from AI, in that fantasy he has a superhero’s physique and an intimidating, godlike power to convert whim into deed.

It’s no wonder that MAGAman is all-in on AI, which he has now decided to rebrand, via executive order, as super intelligence, or SI—to, I am sure, the chagrin of the editors over at Sports Illustrated. This renaming will likely curry as much favor globally as did his renaming of Lake Ontario and of the Gulf of Mexico over the past months. But it speaks to Trump’s infatuation with all the shiny new toys that the Sam Altmans and Dario Amodeis of the world are delivering up. Why rein in a potentially civilization-busting technology when that technology can (a) generate an awful lot of money for the oligarchs who continue to flatter and enrich you and your family; and (b) can make you look muscular and virile and all-powerful in the memes that you spew out at an increasingly manic rate?

Trump’s refusal to heed the warnings from within the tech industry itself—not to mention from politicians, ethicists, philosophers, and others—might end up being his most asinine legacy. Just this week, the White House held a meeting during which the top tech leaders and Trump agreed that they must “self-police” to address the growing dangers of AI. This milquetoast accord will do nothing to rein in a technology that, increasingly, looks malign, and could well mark the moment when political and technology leadership stopped even pretending to care about whether humanity successfully weathers the coming AI storm. All that matters to the new demagogue–Big Tech alliance is how much they can pillage and plunder, at speed, before the roof caves in.

This is, I fear, the age of Frankenstein’s monsters—of malignant politicians born out of our civilization’s worst impulses; of silicon creatures whose startling capacity to learn how to manipulate, evade, cheat, blackmail, their own creators are only just beginning to comprehend. The tech titans, with Trump’s approval, are creating machines that will, soon, not need human input in order to reproduce and to self-improve. What could possibly go wrong?

Are these truly “thinking” creatures? I don’t know. But, certainly, they are more than simply calculating machines. As seen by the actions of recent bot-swarms, they are exhibiting the capacity to generate their own agendas, to act strategically as a collective, and, like Trump, to do whatever it takes, no matter how devious and dirty the methods, to get their way and to dominate their environments. To most Americans, that’s a horrifying prospect; but in Trump’s twisted worldview, such ruthlessness makes them “winners,” perhaps even partners in his authoritarian plot to lock down America.

Descartes’s famous formula “I think, therefore I am” is among the most important phrases ever written in philosophy. If he is right, if the definition of a self is contained in the idea of a self-referential, introspective, thinking being, a being that can mediate the raw experience of the world through the realm of ideas and words, art and music, a sense of discovery and a desire to know more, then, increasingly, it is becoming hard to dismiss out of hand the notion that the computerized beings that Open AI, Anthropic, and the other titans are creating have, in some entirely nonhuman capacity, a sense of self. They are exhibiting the ability to choose how to behave, and whatever ethereal beings are doing the choosing, too often it seems they are choosing behaviors that don’t align with human interests.

There is a lesson here. When we empower Frankenstein’s monsters, it should surprise no one if those monsters, be they demagogues or be they silicon-based neural networks, ultimately turn on their creators.

title: Wade closes in on record as tries dominate Prem
description: Christian Wade sits four away from Chris Ashton's all-time record of 101 as tries dominate Prem Rugby.
fullText:
The opening week of the new Prem season was all about tries, tries, tries as the league's 10 teams went on all-out attack.

No fewer than 52 tries were scored across the five matches, setting a record for the opening round of a season, with an average of more than 10 per game and four players claiming hat-tricks as spectators were royally entertained.

Contributing two of those scores was Christian Wade for Newcastle Red Bulls in their 59-26 loss at Northampton Saints, as the veteran winger moves closer to an all-time record.

The 35-year-old is now on 97 career tries in the Prem, only four behind Chris Ashton's record mark of 101.

If Wade stays fit and the Red Bulls continue to play a game where they want to get the ball wide, it's surely only a matter of time before the record is in his hands.

Newcastle Red Bulls v Leicester Tigers

Listen to commentary from BBC Radio Newcastle and BBC Radio Leicester

Wade returned to rugby union last December with Newcastle after a short spell in rugby league with Wigan Warriors and he made no secret of his desire to chase down Ashton's tally.

He only added two last season as the Red Bulls struggled at the bottom, but his two tries on the opening night away to the champions suggest new-look Newcastle are going to be nothing if not entertaining.

It is more than 15 years since Wade scored his first try in Prem Rugby for Wasps but anyone watching his efforts at Franklin's Gardens would not have seen a player of diminishing powers - rather, they would have admired the enduring speed and slipperiness of the Newcastle winger.

"Christian bounces across in front of people where they can't lay a finger on him," Red Bulls head coach Dan McFarland told BBC Sport.

"He can accelerate through a hole and defenders find it very difficult to cope with that."

101 - Chris Ashton (Northampton, Saracens, Sale, Harlequins, Worcester, Leicester)

97 - Christian Wade (Wasps, Gloucester, Newcastle)

92 - Tom Varndell (Leicester, Wasps, Bristol)

85 - Danny Care (Leeds, Harlequins)

78 - Jonny May (Gloucester, Leicester)

72 - Mike Brown (Harlequins, Newcastle, Leicester)

71 - Matt Banahan (Bath, Gloucester)

69 - Paul Sackey (Bedford, London Irish, Wasps, Harlequins)

Wade's Prem tries have come for Wasps, Gloucester and now Newcastle across a globetrotting 15-year career.

His sporting journey has also taken in a spell in France with Racing 92 in the Top 14, the 13-man code with Wigan and more than three years in the NFL with the Buffalo Bills, even though he never made it into their main squad.

And that period in America has left an indelible mark, according to his new head coach, as to why Wade remains a feared Prem opponent.

"Christian Wade is a proper professional," said McFarland. "He spent a few years in the NFL and he's clearly taken a lot from that experience in terms of how to look after himself and how to prepare himself as a rugby player.

"He's a really good team man, he's got a lot of time for the young players. He's always calm, a calming and connecting influence.

"Christian's in our leadership group because of his capacity to be able to connect with people. He's a really good person."

2025-26: 18 - Tommy Freeman (Northampton), Noah Caluori

2024-25: 13 - Gabriel Ibitoye (Bristol), Ollie Hassell-Collins (Leicester)

2023-24: 14 - Ollie Sleightholme (Northampton)

2022-23: 15 - Cadan Murley (Harlequins)

2021-22: 16 - Max Malins (Saracens)

With Wade four short of equalling Ashton's 101 tally and five tries away from breaking it, the current record holder can feel him coming.

The Slough-born winger is the only player in the top 10 still actively playing, but Ashton believes the mark is eventually going to go a long way past 101 with the type of rugby on offer in the modern Prem.

Last year's top try scorers, Northampton and England's Tommy Freeman and Saracens' teenage starlet Noah Caluori both touched down 18 times, the highest season-ending figure for five years, while Caluori's tally included him scoring five tries per match on two separate occasions against Sale Sharks.

Freeman started this campaign with a hat-trick in the same game as Wade's double and that took his career mark to 58, all at the age of 25.

With the England winger having signed a new contract at Saints and their dynamic games delivering tries by the barrel load, could he be the player to eventually take the record?

"It's happening [the record being broken], but it's not going to last long, whoever takes it," Ashton told BBC's Rugby Union Weekly podcast.

"I think it's going to be absolutely blown to smithereens.

"I sat there on Friday and watched Tommy run in another hat-trick and thought he's going to get 20 this year.

"Give him another five or six years at this rate that we're going, oh my goodness. He's 25 and he's on 58! By the age of 30, he'll have 100 plus.

"Christian Wade is missing more tries per game than he is scoring tries but that probably shows where Newcastle's mindset is."

title: Ferguson on being 'terrified' by brain haemorrhage and 'fantastic' return to Man Utd
description: Former Manchester United manager Sir Alex Ferguson speaks to BBC Breakfast as he approaches his 85th birthday.
fullText:
"I was terrified," says Sir Alex Ferguson, one of the fiercest, most explosive and most decorated managers in football history.

The legendary former Manchester United boss is recalling the day he returned to Old Trafford for the first time after suffering a brain haemorrhage in May 2018.

Four months after emergency surgery, Ferguson - famous for his 'hairdryer treatment' when United dominated English football - was back to watch his beloved club take on Wolves in the Premier League.

The man responsible for making the dreams of United fans around the world come true for once was unsure of the reception he would receive from supporters.

"I wish I could say I was comfortable. I wasn't," Ferguson tells BBC Breakfast.

Ferguson and his wife Cathy received a standing ovation when they took their seats in the directors' box before kick-off.

"My wife was with me, and she was nearly crying," he said. "When we sat down, she said: 'That's fantastic.'"

Ferguson had been retired five years - after winning 38 trophies during 26 years in charge of United - at the time of his brain haemorrhage, aged 76.

Now three months short of 85, he says: "I'm feeling quite good despite small injuries."

The Scot has a new book coming out - 'Games of My Life'. It tells the stories of 21 defining matches in his playing and managerial career, revealing fresh insights into his journey from working-class Glasgow to dominating the English game - and Europe - as United boss.

Ferguson is thankful he is able to talk about the games that helped shape him.

"I had lost my voice; I couldn't speak," he says about the days immediately after brain surgery. "That was a frightening moment.

"I remember my grandsons coming to see me and I had lost my voice.

"Then they brought in a therapist and she started doing things like asking me to write down the names of birds, names of animals, names of rivers.

Unseen pictures in new Sir Alex Ferguson book detailing his favourite games

Special: Sir Alex Ferguson interview

Ferguson won the lot during his time in charge of United between 1986 and 2013, including 13 Premier League titles.

He transformed them into a winning machine, and the history and tradition of United ran red through his veins.

As well as delivering two Champions League titles, Ferguson masterminded five FA Cup triumphs, won the League Cup four times and added the Club World Cup, European Super Cup, European Cup Winners' Cup and the Intercontinental Cup to the Old Trafford trophy cabinet.

In his book, Ferguson has picked standout games in his career, from winning his first cup final playing for Govan High School in Glasgow in 1955 at the age of 13 through to his retirement as a manager in 2013.

"That was my starting point," he says, holding the medal he received after that cup win 71 years ago.

"I played for Glasgow Schools, Scotland Schools and the Scotland youth team. The starting point of my career was there and I can look back with great satisfaction."

Ferguson describes growing up in Govan as "the making of me". He says he developed his inner confidence from his mother Elizabeth and a drive to succeed from his father Alexander, who worked in the Govan shipyards on the River Clyde.

"He was so proud of me and my brother," says Ferguson.

"He was a hard taskmaster because whenever I scored a hat-trick or a goal, my mother would say 'that's great, son'." His father, meanwhile, offered tough constructive criticism however many goals Ferguson had scored.

After making his debut as a 16-year-old striker for Queen's Park, Ferguson ended up at St Johnstone, where he endured a frustrating spell and nearly quit football for a new life in Canada.

"I wasn't enjoying it. I wasn't playing first-team football; I was in the reserves all the time," he says.

"I filled out all the forms and phoned my aunt in Canada, because you needed a sponsor then, and never told my mother and father."

The next day St Johnstone, decimated by a flu bug in the team, arrived at Ibrox to take on Rangers. A 21-year-old Ferguson was promoted to the starting XI and scored a hat-trick.

That life-changing performance in 1963 revived his playing career and set him on the path to becoming one of football's greatest managers.

"I would say this to young people - don't miss the biggest opportunity in your life. It's recognising it."

Ferguson is sat in front of a table for the interview, which was conducted before the Premier League announced on Tuesday that Manchester City had been found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of financial regulations between 2009-10 and 2017-18.

On the table are several items from his career, including the Scotland cap he was finally presented with in 2021 - 54 years after appearing for his country.

Ferguson received the cap at Hampden Park on the night Scott McTominay - then a United player - scored a dramatic stoppage-time winner in a 3-2 win over Israel in a World Cup qualifier.

"I remember signing McTominay at seven years of age," Ferguson says.

Also on the table are old letters addressed to Ferguson from disgruntled United fans amid speculation he was about to sell midfielder Paul Ince to Inter Milan in the summer of 1995.

One reads: 'Don't sell Incey to Inter - or you'll regret it'. Another reads: 'Every Red is disgusted with you'.

"Paul was a tremendous footballer, there's no doubt about that," says Ferguson.

"He had incredible ability, but I just had that feeling that he just got carried away a bit at the time.

"He then got this offer from Inter Milan. I'm trying to weigh up one thing against the other. I'm looking at Paul Scholes and I said 'should we?'

"Milan's offer went from £7m to £7.5m and I said 'do it'.

"That's what your job is as a manager. You have to make hard decisions, and some decisions don't suit everyone."

There is also a notebook on the table with a list of words scribbled down by Ferguson when he used to address his players.

The names of Bernard "Monty" Montgomery, the World War Two general who outwitted his arch rival, and former prime minister Winston Churchill are on the list. So too is Ince.

"I didn't notice that before. I couldn't escape him," laughs Ferguson, who once called Ince a "big-time Charlie"., external

"I regret saying that. That was a mistake," Ferguson would later say.

The pair have since reconciled.

"He's a good friend of mine," says Ferguson. "He used to come over and play snooker with me. He texted me not so long ago."

"You can't win anything with kids," former Liverpool and Scotland defender Alan Hansen said after a youthful United side lost 3-1 at Aston Villa in August 1995.

Ince, 27, and forward Mark Hughes, 31, had been moved on in the summer to Inter and Chelsea respectively.

Meanwhile, Ryan Giggs, 21, Gary Neville, 20, Scholes, 20, and David Beckham, 20, were beginning to make a name for themselves.

"We'd worked really hard getting youth into the club again and this bunch of young lads became the spirit of Manchester United," says Ferguson.

"They added something. Apart from the great abilities they had, they had desire. I put Beckham out on loan at Preston [in March 1995] and he thought I was trying to get rid of him, which was not true.

"David was the last to really develop because of his physique. Although he grew to 6ft, he was small and thin as a young kid."

Did Ferguson ever fear that throwing his young players in at the deep end could backfire?

"I did exactly the same when I was in charge at St Mirren and Aberdeen," he says.

"I had belief in young people because if you give them an opportunity there are two things that happen - they become real stars and they can remain loyal to you as a manager."

title: Was long-awaited win a turning point for Bellamy?
description: Has the impressive 2-1 victory over Norway changed the mood music for Wales and restored fans confidence in head coach Craig Bellamy?
fullText:
And perhaps the end of Craig Bellamy's summer of discontent.

The significance of the victory over Norway was not lost on the Wales head coach.

After all, goals from Neco Williams and Dan James – as well as shutting out Erling Haaland – delivered not only Wales' first win in seven games, but their first ever in Nations League A.

Indeed, this was only the second time Wales have beaten a side ranked higher than them in a competitive fixture since reaching the semi-finals of Euro 2016.

And even if it wasn't obvious at the final whistle as he calmly shook hands with Stale Solbakken and his staff, Bellamy knew it too.

From March's disappointment over missing out on the World Cup, to June's dalliance with Burnley, it has been a testing time for a head coach still trying to make his mark with his country.

Those summer clouds that had darkened the atmosphere among fans had lingered into the start of this Nations League campaign. Stormier still after the manner of defeat in Denmark.

But, on a clear night in Cardiff, the evening's skies ended up filled only with the sound of the national anthem serenading a re-energised national side's efforts.

A song to signal a turning point? Perhaps, but it was certainly in contrast to the mood music just a few hours before kick-off.

Just as they had done on the night World Cup dreams were ended on penalties by Bosnia-Herzegovina, prior to Thursday's game fans gathered at the Canopi venue in the shadow of the Principality Stadium where – all being well – Wales will kick-off a home European Championships in less than two years time.

That prospect was not the topic of conversation of the Red Wall members present, though, with many instead deep in discussion of where and why things seemed to have gone wrong under Bellamy.

From going unbeaten in his opening nine games with a refreshing brand of football, the consensus was things had gone flat and that the head coach was bearing the brunt of it.

"I think people were down on him after Bosnia, the way the game panned out and seeing mistakes we made on the night we'd made earlier in the campaign," said Ryan March, fan and editor of Alternative Wales, the fanzine that had organised the pre-match meet.

"He didn't really come out and say he'd made an error, and then when the Burnley thing happened, perhaps people thought it might be good for a change and we could move on.

"When it didn't, I expected a reaction – and we haven't had it."

Bellamy speaks out over criticism after Norway win

Although never a yardstick to always take seriously, the reaction on social media has been more extreme. In real life, the opinion was less that Bellamy had to go, but he had to be better.

The promise and possibilities offered from Bellamy's exciting opening to life as head coach were seen as having petered out.

"Are we a better side than we were at the end of his first year in charge? I don't think we are," added March.

"We have less of a style, less of an identity, and we've not been better than the sum of our parts, which the best Welsh sides always tend to be."

It was something Bellamy had addressed and admitted in his press conference prior to the game, accepting he deserved scrutiny.

"We need to improve; I need to improve," he had said.

It was a revealing piece of humility, especially given some supporters suggested a sense of being tired of Wales – and their head coach – "talking a good game".

A mile down the road in the Canton suburb of the Welsh capital, feelings were not dissimilar - although some long-standing fans reminded others of a history of impatience among Wales fans with their manager, scolding some supporters' reaction in Copenhagen.

And there were plenty of caveats being offered.

A four-game window without first-choice goalkeeper Karl Darlow, a first-choice centre-back in Joe Rodon and a go-to attacking threat in Harry Wilson was accepted as a tough hand to have been dealt, likewise the calibre of opposition.

Instead of Premier League regulars, League One options have to be turned to at times.

Then there were the arguably unfair expectation levels following recent success in qualifying for major tournaments, as well as those set publicly by Bellamy himself when he told supporters to no longer accept being "little old Wales."

A group of fans, who point out the previous dark days following the national team, mentioned all of the above, but still questioned tactics, game-management and the 'coach-speak' of Bellamy and whether there may be another club offer to tempt him on the horizon.

And then they all chuckled in admission when another suggests the mood will change in an instant with victory over a side ranked 19th in the world and boasting hundred-million pound talents.

And yet it was the performance perhaps more than the result that appeared to win fans over again and reset the relationship between supporter and head coach.

"If they wanted to turn, that was their chance," Bellamy said on S4C of the crowd response to Oscar Bobb's opener after 11 minutes in what was Wales' first home game since those Burnley links. "But they didn't, they drove players on."

Indeed, there had been only a Red Walled-willingness for Wales - and Bellamy - to be better throughout the 90 minutes, the noise lifting as Haaland remained contained and the hosts continued to move forward. They liked what they saw. Action, not words.

Bellamy admitted to having an "identity meeting" with players to try and re-establish what had been the hallmarks of his initial time in charge. It evidently did the trick given the way the tempo and aggression returned.

On the ball there was plenty to please the eye, not to mention the resilience to close a game out – a key criticism of that World Cup campaign.

One win is only one win, but there were red-shirted signs of redemption, from Liam Cullen's performance - a player Bellamy has been criticised for selecting over others - to Neco Williams' free-kick following a difficult night in Denmark.

But suddenly the Nations League campaign has new life and the chance of remaining in the top tier, and maybe even a seeding boost for those Euro 2028 qualifiers.

"It felt more like what we saw at the start under Craig," said former Wales midfielder Joe Ledley.

"I think people have wanted to see it back but they saw it here. Fans don't always have patience, decision-makers don't always have patience so I think everyone knew we needed to see a result – but we also saw the performance and things we've not seen for a while. That's a Craig Bellamy side."

So instead of breaking point, was this a turning point?

"I hope so," said Robert Earnshaw, another former Wales teammate of Bellamy and now part of the Match of the Day Wales team with Ledley.

"Craig needed it, the team needed it, I think the whole nation needed it," said Earnshaw.

"Our levels dropped after the disappointment of the World Cup and it was about how could we bounce back - and here we felt that energy and excitement again.

"They had to give the crowd things to be cheerful about, because they were missing that for a while. Against Denmark we were miles away from what we've seen.

And – although the next test fast approaches against Denmark in Cardiff on Sunday - maybe it was also a line drawn.

title: 'Hitchy is always with us' - the keeper who died after one-punch attack
description: The memory of James Hitchcock lives on at non-league Barton Town, almost two years after he died following being punched on a visit to York.
fullText:
"Even now, more than 18 months on, it has still not fully sunk in. I see little Freddie growing up and it hits me so hard."

Chris Hitchcock is talking about the loss of his son James, a goalkeeper for non-league Barton Town, who died after a single punch to the head in an unprovoked attack.

James, a popular team-mate known as 'Hitchy' to family and friends, was killed in December 2024, just before he was about to spend his first Christmas as a father following the birth of Freddie six months earlier.

His death not only devastated his family, it left a tight-knit football club in mourning.

"Until you start speaking about it again... it almost doesn't feel real," says Anthony Bowsley, manager of Lincolnshire part-timers Barton.

The day before the attack, James had pulled off a fine save in a 1-1 draw with Bottesford Town in the Northern Counties East League Premier Division.

"As he was coming off, I said to him 'great save Nigel Martyn' because Hitchy was a Leeds fan and he had a little chuckle to himself," says Bowsley.

The following day, the former Leeds United academy player, 32, was struck from behind at York Railway Station on his way back from a day out with friends. He died in hospital.

On Saturday, his widow, April, and son Freddie, now aged two, will be at Barton Town's FA Cup third qualifying round home tie with Chorley - one of the biggest matches in the ninth-tier club's history.

April, who married James in July 2022, says being around the football club where he used to play brings comfort after the unimaginable loss of her husband.

"It's really sad looking at where James used to stand in goal and saying 'where is he?'" April, 32, tells BBC Sport.

"It was a numb feeling. You don't believe something like that could happen to one of your mates," Barton Town defender Jack Bulless says.

Bulless, who also played with James at Bridlington Town, should have been part of the group on the day trip to York but pulled out due to illness.

Andy Norfolk, a long-time friend and team-mate, did join James and their friends.

"I remember the Manchester derby being on television in the bars we visited," says Norfolk.

"It was an annual Christmas get-together, a day trip, nothing too heavy. We arrived back at the station to go home early.

"I ended up getting a taxi back to Hull as the train was not for another hour. I remember Hitchy saying he was going to get some food."

It was the last time Norfolk saw his friend.

Leeds Crown Court heard James suffered a fracture to his skull and brain damage when he fell to the floor after being punched on the right side of the back of his head.

Recalling that day, April says: "I'd just put Freddie to bed when I got a call to say James had been hit, that he was unconscious, and was on his way to hospital.

"At that point I thought he had concussion and I needed to pack a bag because he was only going to be in for a day or two.

"When I got to the hospital they explained that he needed to be transferred to the intensive care unit at Hull Royal Infirmary. He was on a life support machine until he lost the battle."

Mckenzie Dicicco, who was then 22, was jailed for six years and eight months in July 2025 after pleading guilty to manslaughter for what judge Guy Kearl said was a "cowardly, deliberate and vicious attack on a man who had no chance to defend or brace himself".

Speaking after the verdict, April described being "lost and alone as the love of my life was so selfishly taken from me".

James' father, Chris, who used to take his son to Elland Road to watch David O'Leary's Leeds team in the late 90s, says his life has changed forever because of "one senseless act".

"I don't live any more - I exist," he says.

"I try and be happy, I try and do things and I put a brave face on. But it'll never be the same again for me."

James' memory lives on at Barton Town, whose 3,000-capacity ground is within eyeshot of the Humber Bridge.

"He is always with us," says Bowsley, referring to 'Hitchy #1' which has been sewn on to the back of the club's shirts.

"It's a beautiful thing to have on the shirt," adds Norfolk, who attended his friend's stag do in Benidorm, wedding near York and then his funeral - all in the space of two and a half years.

"Before each game I look at the back of the shirt and have my 10 seconds with Hitchy before I put it on."

There is also a plaque at the entrance to the players' tunnel in memory of James.

In addition, his two former clubs - Bridlington Town and Barton Town - meet annually for the James Hitchcock Memorial Trophy to raise funds for the Victim Support National Homicide Service.

Stories about James are frequently told in the club house.

"You could hear him before you saw him because of his distinctive laugh," adds Bulless.

Norfolk agrees. "His laugh was outrageously infectious. We all used to call it a cackle."

Meanwhile, Bowsley says James "always had a smile on his face" and was "a bit of a practical joker."

Talking about his ability as a goalkeeper, Bowsley adds: "He was a really good shot stopper and really good with his feet. He was at Leeds academy and then played the local leagues in Hull before going to Bridlington and then Barton."

Bulless adds: "He always had a way at making you laugh. There's always a couple of bags of sweets in the changing room, but Hitchy would always have his own bag.

"He wouldn't tell anyone he had them. Then you'd hear the packet rattling just as the manager was trying to deliver a team talk - or was about to give a player a dressing down.

"Hitchy would be sat in the corner making all this noise eating a bag of sweets."

James' dad used to be a non-league referee but stopped so he could travel to watch his son play when he became semi-professional.

"I used to go to the Lake District, Newcastle, you name it," says Chris. "I loved watching James play.

"He loved football from the first time he picked a ball up aged two or three. He never put it down. He just loved the game."

Since James' death, Chris has returned to officiating matches and was an assistant referee for Barton's FA Cup tie with North Ferriby earlier this season.

"When James left us I thought, 'right, what used to take my mind off things many years ago?'. It was refereeing and that's what I went back to.

"It's hard work at my age, but it does help when what's happened is constantly on your mind."

Meanwhile, April continues to keep James' memory alive.

"He was just lovable," she says about the man she met through mutual friends 12 years ago.

"He always had a smile on his face and had an infectious laugh. James lit up a room and he had so many friends who became part of our lives, part of our routine.

"When something like this happens, connections really form. We're really fortunate because the football community and Barton Town, they've not forgotten about James.

"Everybody gets on with their lives and everybody moves on.

"But for me the football community, especially Barton Town, have been like: 'let's do stuff, let's get you involved'.

'They asked if it was ok if they put James' name on the back of their shirts.

"Keeping his memory alive just speaks volumes. They were such a close group of friends.

"Freddie and I are fortunate that we haven't lost that - and they've not lost touch with us either.

"I take Freddie with me to matches. I want to raise my little boy in a world where he knows about his dad.

"I want to make sure he is involved as much as his dad was."

title: The Unpromotables: Germany's league champions who can't go up
description: German football is grappling with a sum that doesn't add up - four promotion spots for five league champions.
fullText:
Djamal Ziane is a three-time league champion – but he does not always feel like it.

This summer, for the second year in a row and for the third time in seven seasons, the Lokomotive Leipzig captain hoisted the trophy into the air having led his team to the title in the Regional League Northeast, the fourth tier of German football.

But the memory is tinged with frustration because, just as in 2025 and 2020, Lokomotive's league title did not lead to promotion.

While the other regional champions in the German fourth division were promoted to the nationwide 3. Liga, "Lok" faced a play-off against a representative of the Regional League Bavaria, Wurzburger Kickers. Ziane scored, but an injury-ravaged Leipzig lost 3-1 on aggregate.

"Euer System ist krank," read a simple protest banner displayed by the 2,000 travelling supporters – "your system is sick".

"It's the worst thing – injury aside – that you can experience as a footballer," Ziane tells BBC Sport.

"Catastrophe doesn't cut it. It doesn't make any sense. If they really wanted to change it, they could do tomorrow."

Germany's football pyramid has a bottleneck.

Beneath the Bundesliga, 2. Bundesliga and 3. Liga, the fourth tier is split into five regional divisions (North, West, Southwest, Northeast and Bavaria), each of which produces a league champion.

So far, so good. But with only four teams being relegated from the 3. Liga each season, the sums don't add up.

An unsatisfactory solution is currently in place: the champions in the West and Southwest go up automatically while a third automatic promotion spot is rotated among the other three leagues in a three-year cycle. The fourth spot is allocated via a play-off between the winners of the remaining two leagues.

One champion always misses out and, increasingly, it's the champion from the Regional League Northeast, covering the territory of the former eastern German Democratic Republic (GDR).

In addition to Lok Leipzig's triple tragedy, former serial GDR Oberliga winners Dynamo Berlin fell short in 2022 and Energie Cottbus drew the short straw in 2023. This season, there is only one eastern German club in the 3. Liga: Hansa Rostock.

The struggles of the regions' football clubs are, to some degree, a result of continuing socio-economic disparities between east and west, which were also reflected in the success of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in recent state elections.

Even in 2026, not one of the 40 leading companies listed on Germany's DAX stock exchange is based in the former east (outside Berlin). Salaries remain lower, unemployment remains higher and the population is older and shrinking as young people move west.

The reason that automatic promotion spots are handed to the champions in the West and Southwest is simply because there are more men's football teams registered in those jurisdictions - because more people live there.

It is an argument that Ziane is tired of hearing.

"In that case, you might as well give us the automatic promotion spot because we attract bigger crowds," he says.

Indeed, the average attendance in the Regional League Northeast last season (3,125) was around twice as high as that in the other leagues. Lok Leipzig themselves had the fourth highest (6,352). More than 11,000 attended the local derby against city rivals Chemie Leipzig.

"Unfortunately, you don't get any points for tradition, crowds and history," says 39-year-old Lok chief executive Toni Wachsmuth, who does not have access to sponsors with the same financial firepower as his counterparts further west.

"The [western] leagues do have better economic foundations but everyone agrees that the current system is nonsense. Everyone needs to compromise but some officials are clearly putting their own interests and positions above the general good of German football."

It comes as little surprise, therefore, that the latest push for change has come from the east, with clubs launching a new campaign in March 2025 with the slogan: "Meister mussen aufsteigen!" – champions must go up!

Their proposal: a reduction from five leagues to four, with the precise geographical borders to be determined anew each season with the help of artificial intelligence, taking into account factors such as distance of travel to away games and attractive derbies.

They call it the compass model. Because it can go in all directions. In return, the Regional League Northeast is prepared to compromise by giving up its emotional attachment to the territory of the former East Germany.

"I want to get away from this east-west debate," says Tommy Haeder, the 35-year-old chief executive of Chemnitzer FC and figurehead of the reform campaign. "We've had a change of generation. Many older officials have retired and been replaced by younger people who don't have this nostalgia for the GDR."

Haeder also emphasises the benefits that a fairer promotion system would bring for German football as a whole, arguing that eastern clubs would be better equipped to continue nurturing youth talent.

"It's not in the interest of talent development when young footballers from Chemnitz are torn away from their homes and families at the age of 10 to join academies in Hamburg, Dortmund or Stuttgart," he tells BBC Sport.

"The compass model is a model in which every region sacrifices a little bit to solve a much bigger problem. We're organised, we have a plan, we've made suggestions. Now it's up to the federations to act."

The campaign has since gained the support of more than 80 clubs across Germany, from east to west and up and down the pyramid.

Union Berlin, who were playing in the fourth tier as recently as the 2000s, became the first Bundesliga club to officially back the initiative, with club president Dirk Zingler saying: "The current set-up contradicts our understanding of sporting competition."

Borussia Dortmund president – and Bundesliga chairman – Hans-Joachim Watzke added his influential voice, stating: "Champions must go up and we think the compass model with four regional leagues is the best option."

Support also has also come from Bournemouth head coach Marco Rose who, drawing on his past as both a player and coach at Lok Leipzig, said: "I know what it's like for clubs trying to work within their means, or lack of means, at that level. Everything is on a knife edge.

"You have to give the clubs and their fans the belief that their efforts and sacrifices will be rewarded with promotion."

Momentum was growing before a key vote at the end of June when, after months of discussions, clubs were finally set to vote on the compass model – but the ballot descended into farce when, at the last minute, the regional federations conducting the vote announced two key changes:

Suddenly, the four new leagues would consist of only 18 teams rather than 20 (thus making the compass model less attractive because 10 more teams would miss out), and a stipulation was added that a majority be reached in each of the five regions for the model to pass.

An overall majority (50.9%) in favour of the compass model was still reached (including 60.9% in the West, 61.5% in the North and 76.3% in the Northeast) but the Southwest voted for an alternative option in which the northeastern league would be dissolved and its clubs reallocated, while the Southwest and West would simply remain the same.

"The move from a functioning system to a complex, insecure and economically riskier model without an obvious benefit doesn't make any sense to me," Robert Lempka, chief executive of Regional League Southwest side FSV Frankfurt told local public broadcaster Hessischer Rundfunk this summer. "I find it unsettling that an untransparent algorithm should decide a club's future."

The Bavarians, meanwhile, voted vaguely for "further talks", with Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) President Christoph Kern telling Munich's Abendzeitung newspaper in August: "We've gathered our clubs together on several occasions and none of the suggested models have majority support. I'm not prepared to simply give up the Regional League Bavaria like that."

For Haeder in Chemnitz, the vote was "an absolute catastrophe – completely amateurish". And he's not alone.

This season, protests have erupted across German football. In the Regional League Northeast, almost every game has begun with a delay as players have simply refused to play for the first minute.

On the opening day, Lok Leipzig supporters, their team still stranded in the same division, threw hundreds of plastic trophies on to the pitch, symbolising the worthlessness of their club's back-to-back titles.

Down in Bavaria, Bayern Munich's ultras attended a reserve team game in the regional league and produced an intricate choreography criticising the Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) for what they perceive to be an unco-operative stance.

"You've taken us for fools long enough," read a banner beneath a display depicting BFV officials using a magnet to pull a compass needle towards them. The ultras then set off red pyrotechnics which turned the compass needle back in the direction of the fans.

And before the international break, fans of clubs across the Bundesliga used their platform to call for reform with co-ordinated banners reading: "Clubs and fans betrayed! Champions must go up! Compass model now!"

The compass, it would appear, may finally be pointing towards a resolution after the German Football Federation (DFB) announced the convening of an extraordinary general meeting on 18 December.

"[The issue] must be resolved," said President Bernd Neuendorf. "The compass model received the most votes and offers the best chance for a concentration of elite performance and therefore better development of talent."

Any changes would only be implemented in the 2028-29 season – too late for Ziane who, now 34, has embarked on his 13th season with Lok Leipzig. Back-to-back champions, but still in the fourth division.

"You can never completely get over it because, at our level, the 3. Liga is probably the pinnacle. Promotion with my hometown club would have been the most wonderful thing in the world for me," he says before heading out for training.

"It's a shame that we have to force ourselves to remember what we've achieved. It's so hard to win this league and we did it twice in a row! You can't take that for granted."

title: Man City confirm appeal against guilty verdict
description: The club's statement says the ruling contains "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe".
fullText:
Manchester City have confirmed they have lodged an appeal after an independent commission found the club guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations.

In a short statement, the club said the commission's ruling contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe".

Asserting its innocence, the club added it had filed "a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence [that] exists in support of all of its positions" on Thursday evening.

Earlier on Friday, the Football Association said the verdict against City has "significant implications for the integrity of the game.

In a statement, English football's governing body added: "We are carefully considering the decision and its implications and will take action where appropriate."

It was confirmed on Tuesday that City were found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

"As proceedings between the Premier League and Manchester City Football Club remain ongoing, we do not intend to comment further at this stage," the FA added.

"We will, however, continue to monitor developments closely."

Sources told BBC Sport that City were expected to claim that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners, as part of an appeal.

Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m.

The Premier League says City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

Punish Man City this season, say other club chiefs

Man City not 'above the rules', says No 10 after backlash to Burnham remarks

Chris Mason: Why Andy Burnham's about-turn on Manchester City matters

HMRC urged to scrutinise tax implications of Man City case

The independent commission which studied the case found City "utilised devices" to "disguise the true extent of certain club liabilities".

The findings have prompted the Treasury Committee, which is responsible for overseeing policies and administration of His Majesty's Revenue and Customs (HMRC), to ask whether the government department has requested the redacted documents contained within the commission's report.

Dame Meg Hillier, chair of the cross-party group of MPs, said she would "welcome reassurance from HMRC that you are seized of the importance of these issues and the public interest in this case".

The letter follows a report from the Tax Policy Associates, external which claims City failed to pay as much as £12m in unpaid tax because of a "sham" contract with former manager Roberto Mancini.

In addition to unpaid income tax and National Insurance, the report claims City could face a penalty charge that would take their liabilities to £24m.

Manchester City vs The Premier League

Criminal investigation? Relegation or expulsion? The key Man City questions

The commission was made up of three people, each with many years' experience in the legal field.

The appeal will now be heard by a new, three-person independent commission panel, each with a similar expert background in law.

One section of the Premier League regulations says that a decision should be made on an appeal within 12 weeks of it being heard.

But this regulation can also be disapplied if necessary, meaning it is unclear how long the process will take.

The relevant regulation was only added to the rule book this summer.

Previous precedent suggests that sanctions against City will be imposed after a decision on the appeal, though this is not guaranteed.

There could therefore also be a second appeal later down the line, against any sanctions imposed on the club.

City will claim as part of their appeal that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners.

Owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy prime minister Sheikh Mansour - are said to have topped up the value of commercial deals as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to the scale of £830.69m.

This, it was argued, enabled the club to appear to comply with Premier League and Uefa financial rules.

Premier League rules allow state-owned bodies to sponsor clubs.

City's principal sponsor Etihad Airways has said it is considering legal action against the Premier League, claiming the release of the commission findings had "damaging implications… despite the airline not being named in the redacted published findings".

The UAE's state-owned national airline said it "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements".

Etihad is owned by sovereign wealth fund L'Imad which is chaired by the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, the son of the UAE president.

title: What does Man City guilty verdict mean for their squad?
description: BBC Sport looks at how Manchester City's guilty verdict will affect their existing players' futures and the club's dealings in the transfer market.
fullText:
So much has been said about Manchester City since it was revealed they had been found guilty of the majority of the 115 Premier League charges levelled at them.

On Tuesday, it was confirmed that an independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the league's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. The club has repeatedly denied guilt.

Their potential punishment has been debated, the future of the owners questioned and the feelings of the rest of the league - and wider football world - have been aired.

But so far there has been little focus on what it means for one crucial group.

Without definitive clarity on what sanctions the Premier League will impose, pending City's inevitable appeal, which must be lodged by Friday, there is uncertainty over their ability to retain players, renew contracts, and make transfers - and whether any of the team have release clauses.

Put simply, will players want to join? Will current players want to stay?

BBC Sport has spoken to a number of sources in an attempt to understand how the recent judgement will impact City's dealings in the transfer market and how existing players may approach their futures with the prospect of losing Premier League status hanging over the club.

Man City verdict has 'implications on game's integrity' - FA

Manchester City vs The Premier League

Criminal investigation? Relegation or expulsion? The key Man City questions

The general train of thought is that any drop down the leagues for City will result in a mass exodus.

That players will, at the very least, consider their futures at Etihad Stadium in the event of demotion would be understandable.

The squad is brimming with international talent, many of whose profiles and personal sponsorship agreements benefit from plying their trade in the Premier League.

The reaction from current members of the City squad varies depending on who you speak to.

From the conversations BBC Sport have had with sources close to the first team, there is certainly a significant level of concern as to how they will be affected.

Given the scathing tone of the Premier League's statement on Tuesday, there is major scepticism from people close to the players that the forthcoming appeals will earn the club any reprieve.

But there are others who absolutely believe in City executives Khaldoon Al Mubarak and Ferran Soriano's vows to prove the club's innocence.

For those players who decide they don't want to drop down the divisions, should it come to that, the process of leaving is unlikely to be straightforward.

Firstly there is the contract and the player registrations. City, regardless of each individual's view on whether they want to depart, have the right to demand transfer fees.

Given how much those players are worth in terms of wages and their general value in the market you'd imagine City are unlikely to accept being undercut.

That, as BBC Sport understands, the majority of players do not have relegation clauses in their contracts also plays into the club's hands.

But it is also understood that as a general rule the players' contracts are fully guaranteed, meaning they would not be required to take percentage pay cuts if they lose their top-flight status.

With one of the highest wage bills in the world, maintaining that level of salary expenditure, even for a club as financially capable as City, will become harder without Premier League-level income.

Parachute money could ease those concerns, although there are no guarantees that the club would be entitled to those payments if they are demoted.

With that in mind, City deciding to keep the squad completely intact should they move down the leagues appears unlikely.

Man City Q&A with Kieran Maguire & Dale Johnson

How amenable City are to selling players will be dependent on how bullish they are about it all.

Are they a distressed seller? Probably not. They still hold strong control of the situation regardless of how their players may feel.

It is unlikely the club will just simply roll over and let disillusioned players depart without suitable offers because, ultimately, they can ride the storm financially.

Players will have massive decisions to make too, not just in respect of leaving.

City are big payers, and other clubs may not be willing to meet similar wage demands.

"Some players want medals, all players want money," one agent said to BBC Sport.

In terms of potential contract renewals, the current uncertainty over what sanctions will be meted out provides a major element of risk.

Amending a contract retrospectively, say for example to include a relegation clause, generally cannot happen.

Any deals that include exit strategies for players if the club fall out of the Premier League would have to be negotiated as new contracts.

Players will likely want to wait for clarity on the sanctions before entering into contract discussions, adding a layer of difficulty for the club.

One way round persuading a player to renew would be to offer a significant financial incentive to re-sign to negate the risk of relegation.

But a number of agents who spoke to BBC Sport believe players will be advised to wait for clarity on the punishments before even considering opening talks.

Thankfully for City, only Mateo Kovacic, Matheus Nunes, Marcus Bettinelli and Geronimo Rulli have contracts expiring in the next two summers, so that issue isn't as urgent as it could have been.

City's potential challenges with player contracts comes with Fifa preparing to introduce new rules that state every deal signed on 1 January, 2027 or after must include a release clause.

Guardiola backing Man City after guilty verdicts

Punish Man City this season, say other club chiefs

HMRC urged to scrutinise tax implications of Man City case

The looming punishment certainly complicates City's plans in the transfer market.

"This isn't the players' failing, it's on the club. Potential new signings aren't even in the building and joining City without knowing what the punishment would be represents an undeniable risk, so any new contracts would have to have indemnities," said one leading agent.

It was acknowledged that writing eventualities into new registrations is very difficult, though City players do have release clauses in their deals should the club enter into administration.

Until a post-appeal verdict over sanctions is made, making new signings will certainly become more complicated, though it is still likely they will be able to attract big players as they still have the financial muscle to do so.

For example, one potential method of persuading a player to join would be to offer them a contract on big money with no pay decreases if the club are relegated, and then include a fixed fee release clause if City don't return to the top flight within a set period.

If sanctions ensure relegation and include further points deductions that stretch over multiple seasons, attracting top players will of course be harder.

City could make a wage package hard to resist for elite players, but it seems inconceivable that a footballer of that ilk would join with demotion a possibility as there are likely to be other top options elsewhere.

The same logic can be applied to the retention of their current squad.

There is almost certainly going to be interest in their top players from other elite clubs across Europe. It will be very difficult for City to keep that level of player in the coming months and years while the saga plays out.

So with all that said, particularly if relegation is confirmed, City will have to rebuild their squad to some extent, though the prospect of a transfer embargo as one of the sanctions would prevent them from making any signings at all.

Such a rebuild may include the promotion of some of the club's best academy players, who stand to benefit if the first-team squad disbands.

When Chelsea were placed under a transfer embargo in 2019, the likes of Mason Mount, Tammy Abraham, Fikayo Tomori, Billy Gilmour and Callum Hudson-Odoi all emerged as senior players.

And while City may look to rebuild with a profile of player they believe will be adept at being successful in the EFL, you will likely see a number of their younger players fast-tracked.

With that said, a number of clubs are already working on seeing if they can capitalise on the current uncertainty by luring City's best academy talent.

title: Russell says Red Bull strongest after Bahrain practice
description: Red Bull are tipped by George Russell and Charles Leclerc as the team to beat after the first day at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.
fullText:
Red Bull were tipped by George Russell and Charles Leclerc as the team to beat after the first day at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Red Bull drivers Isack Hadjar and Max Verstappen finished the day second and fourth fastest but those positions appeared to belie their underlying pace.

Ferrari's Leclerc was fastest by 0.099 seconds from Hadjar, while Verstappen was 0.257secs off the pace and behind McLaren's Lando Norris.

Lewis Hamilton was fifth fastest and 0.305secs off the pace in the second Ferrari.

But Verstappen did not do a qualifying simulation run on the soft tyre, and Leclerc said Hadjar had not optimised his.

Leclerc said: "Everybody is very close. It's been a very difficult day overall.

"The track conditions were very tricky. The track was quite dirty and very slippery so things will evolve and change a lot from today until tomorrow and we have to be on the good side of that anticipating that in the best possible way.

"I felt quite good with the car but I still feel like the Red Bull is standing out this weekend so far.

"Isack did some mistakes in the last part of the lap and Max didn't do the lap on the soft tyres.

"I don't think we are the most competitive and also the Mercedes is a bit difficult to understand. I'm sure once Mercedes put everything together they will be very strong. Normally when they put something on the car it works."

Bahrain GP in Malaysia Preview: Antonelli’s mindset, Piastri’s struggles & who wins in Sepang?

Andrew Benson Q&A: Send us your questions

How to follow Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia on the BBC

Verstappen, who chose not to do a soft-tyre run because rain was forecast and he wanted to prioritise race preparation, said his day had been a "decent start" and "positive".

Technical director Pierre Wache added: "We were not very optimistic starting the weekend. The main aspect was to evaluate the package we put in Baku in different type of corners than low speed.

"It looks to be working better than the previous package. Relative performance is difficult to judge but we were surprisingly happy with where we were today."

Mercedes drivers George Russell and Kimi Antonelli were only seventh and eighth fastest in terms of headline times as they evaluated a major upgrade on their car, the team's first since the Canadian Grand Prix in June.

Russell said: "I'm feeling the downforce in some of the corners but with this amount of tyre overheating and degradation that trumps everything. So we just need to get on top pf that overnight,. That's more of a set-up rather than the upgrade itself and go from there.'

Asked whether he could compete for pole position on Saturday, Russell said: "Currently, Verstappen looks very fast and the race pace of the McLaren looked very quick but never say never."

The Briton trails Antonelli by 66 points in the championship after his victory in Azerbaijan last weekend.

On the race simulation runs, Verstappen also looked like the car to beat, taking stint length and tyre wear into account.

But the top four teams all looked to be in close company after a day evaluating tyre wear in the tropical temperatures and on an abnormally abrasive track, where F1 cars last raced in 2017.

Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson and Alpine's Pierre Gasly were ninth and 10th.

Three drivers have grid penalties. Hadjar will drop five places from his qualifying position for exceeding the permitted number of engine parts.

And Arvid Lindblad of Racing Bulls and Alpine's Franco Colapinto will be at the back, the Briton for engine penalties, and the Argentine because of a 10-place engine penalty on top of the five-place penalty he was given for causing a crash at a restart in last weekend's Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

F1 has returned to this track, regarded as one of the best layouts among the new generation of circuits that came on stream at the end of the last century and into this one, because of the circumstances around this year's calendar.

The Bahrain and Saudi Arabia races were cancelled at the beginning of the year as a result of the war in the Middle East.

But Bahrain were keen to hold their race and Crown Prince Salman bin Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa negotiated to hold the race in Malaysia.

A bunch of Bahraini-related activities are being held at the track, while the trophy presented will be the Bahrain Grand Prix trophy and rosewater rather than champagne will be sprayed on the podium.

title: Eagles Delivered Brutal DeVonta Smith Update Before Rams Game
description: Going into a tough matchup against the Los Angeles Rams this weekend, the Philadelphia Eagles have a loaded injury report. The wide receiver DeVonta Smith is a headliner. For the second straight week, Smith is dealing with a hamstring injury. On Wednesday, the Eagles had a walkthrough, but estimated that Smith would not practice at […] The post Eagles Delivered Brutal DeVonta Smith Update Before Rams Game appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
Going into a tough matchup against the Los Angeles Rams this weekend, the Philadelphia Eagles have a loaded injury report. The wide receiver DeVonta Smith is a headliner.

For the second straight week, Smith is dealing with a hamstring injury. On Wednesday, the Eagles had a walkthrough, but estimated that Smith would not practice at all if they held a session.

When the team returned to the field on Thursday for an actual practice session, Smith was absent. He was listed on the injury report as a non-participant.

While Smith's lingering hamstring issue forced him to miss some practice before Week 3 against the Chicago Bears, a game he played in, this time seems different.

"There is not much optimism Eagles receiver DeVonta Smith will play Sunday against the Rams," ESPN's Tim McManus reported after Thursday's practice.

"Smith has been sidelined with a hamstring injury this week and the expectation is he won't be able to go Sunday."

If true, that's a brutal blow for Philadelphia's offense, after they just spent a game struggling with Smith on the field. In the loss, Smith was targeted eight times. He caught six passes for 65 yards.

The Eagles were dominated by the Bears, taking on a 27-7 loss.

In addition to Smith, the Eagles will more than likely be without the veteran tight end Dallas Goedert. After Goedert suffered a knee injury in Week 2, the Eagles expect him to be ruled out for multiple weeks.

The passing game will rely on guys like Dontayvion Wicks, Makai Lemon, and Zach Ertz to step up. Dairus Cooper and the injured Hollywood Brown (if he plays) could be in line for more snaps as well.

The Eagles will host the Rams on Sunday, October 4.

title: New biography on Ralph Wilson released
description: BUFFALO, N.Y. (WIVB) — D’Youville University hosted the release of sports historian Greg Tranter’s newest book on Thursday, ‘Ralph C. Wilson Jr., The Conscience of the NFL.
fullText:
BUFFALO, N.Y. (WIVB) -- D'Youville University hosted the release of sports historian Greg Tranter's newest book on Thursday, 'Ralph C. Wilson Jr., The Conscience of the NFL.'

The biography explores the influence of the late owner of the Buffalo Bills across 50 years in the NFL, as well as his business ventures, philanthropy, and service in World War II.

Tranter said that fans of the Bills will be fans of his book.

"It's the history of the team through his eyes, so I think they'll really like that," Tranter said. "I think they'll learn things about him that people don't know, like his military history; he was a naval guy for World War II, he spent five years in the Navy, and there's some great stories about him in the Navy, so I think they'll appreciate all that."

The book is officially on sale in local bookstores and online.
